For Latter-day Saints, this foreshadows the true Messiah, Jesus Christ, who is anointed by the Father (D&C 65:5) and serves as the perfect High Priest (Hebrews 7:24-28)—but unlike the earthly high priest, Christ needed no purification for Himself.

word_study.meaning: To miss the mark, to violate a command. Here used twice: 'if the priest...sin' and 'for his sin which he hath sinned,' emphasizing that the priest himself is the subject and the victim of his own violation.
word_study.significance: The doubling grammatically insists on personal accountability. The priest cannot hide behind his office or claim the people bear responsibility for his failure. He must bring the offering 'for his sin which he hath sinned'—personal, deliberate acknowledgment.

word_study.meaning: Bringing guilt, contamination, or liability upon the people. The priest's unintentional sin creates collective shame and pollution.
word_study.significance: This phrase explains why the priest's offering procedure is more elaborate than the commoner's: the contamination is deeper and more widespread. The priest's sin reaches into the sanctuary; his purification must therefore penetrate the sanctuary more thoroughly. This principle—contamination spreads according to the offerer's position—governs the entire system.

word_study.meaning: A young bull, calf of cattle. 'Par' is a generic bull; 'ben-baqar' literally 'son of cattle' specifies domestic bovine livestock.
word_study.significance: This is the premium animal. The progression of offerings in Leviticus 4 moves from par (priest, v3) to eil (leader's ram, v23) to chevrah (commoner's female goat, v28). The size and value descend with the offerer's responsibility. The priest's bullock is the most costly testimony to his critical role in Israel's worship.

word_study.meaning: Complete, whole, unblemished; without defect. A standard requirement for sacrificial animals, ensuring that only the finest is offered to God.
word_study.significance: Tamim appears repeatedly in sacrifice requirements (Leviticus 1:3, 3:1, 4:3, etc.) and is extended typologically to moral and spiritual perfection (Deuteronomy 18:13—'be thou perfect with the LORD thy God'). In chata't context, the spotless animal represents the substitution: the perfect substitute bears away the contamination caused by human imperfection.

cross_references.connection: Describes the anointing of Aaron as high priest, the ceremony that makes him 'the anointed priest' referenced here. His anointing sanctified him, but Leviticus 4:3 shows that anointing did not isolate him from the sin-contamination system.

Explicitly interprets the old covenant high priest: 'Every high priest...is compassed with infirmity...for himself, as well as for the people, to offer for sins.' The New Testament commentary confirms that the high priest's own capacity to sin is essential to the typology.

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest brings a bullock as a chata't for himself personally (v3) before presenting offerings for the people (v5). This shows the system's logic: the priest must be purified before he can purify the people.

Identifies Jesus as 'an advocate with the Father' and 'the propitiation for our sins.' Christ is the antitype of the priest who offers for his own people; He needs no separate purification because He is sinless.

The Lord designates the Church president as one who receives revelation and counsels the Church, mirroring the high priest's representative role—with the implication that leadership carries accountability for those they lead.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, the high priest's role was uniquely elevated and uniquely precarious. He alone entered the most holy place (on Yom Kippur, according to Leviticus 16); he alone wore the priestly ephod and breastplate with the Urim and Thummim. His access to divine presence was unparalleled. But access implies responsibility. Ancient societies understood that priestly failure could anger the god and cause the deity to abandon the temple. Israel's system addresses this fear through the chata't: the priest has means to restore purity even when his own sin has contaminated the sanctuary. This is theologically distinctive—the high priest is powerful but not exempt; responsible but not condemned.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi acknowledges his own sins and failings (1 Nephi 8:8, 2 Nephi 4:17-19) despite his role as leader and teacher. The Book of Mormon presents prophets and leaders as participants in the covenant community, subject to the same laws and accountable for their failures. This reflects the principle of Leviticus 4:3: leadership doesn't exempt from the law; it increases accountability.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 107:80-84 specifies that a bishop 'shall be a judge in Zion' with specific powers and duties, but D&C 42:78 warns that bishops who transgress must be dealt with. Like the high priest, the bishop stands in a position of authority but remains subject to God's law. The principle of graduated responsibility runs through Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the presiding authority performs specific ordinances with specific power. But section 84 of Doctrine and Covenants teaches that priesthood power is available through obedience; transgression diminishes authority regardless of office. The high priest in Leviticus 4:3 must bring an offering like any other sinner—the old covenant parallel to the modern principle that personal integrity supports authority.

commentary.christological_typology: The high priest as a type of Christ is developed throughout Hebrew scriptures and fully articulated in Hebrews. But Leviticus 4:3 presents a critical distinction: the earthly high priest 'if...he sin' must bring a purification offering for his own failure. Christ, the perfect High Priest (Hebrews 4:14-16, 7:26-28), is 'without sin' (Hebrews 4:15) and therefore never needs personal purification. His offering is unique: He offers not for His own contamination but as the final, perfect purification for the people. Hebrews 7:27 makes this explicit: 'Who needeth not daily...to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's; for this he did once, when he offered up himself.' The chata't system anticipated a High Priest who would be perfectly obedient where all earthly priests failed.
commentary.application: For those in leadership—priesthood holders, bishops, Relief Society presidents, teachers—this verse teaches that position does not exempt us from the need for repentance and cleansing. In fact, our influence on others' faith increases our accountability. If we lead people astray through our own unintentional lapses, the contamination reaches farther. The remedy is the same: confession, restitution, and a commitment to renewed obedience. For all members, it's a reminder that the highest among us remain human and fallible. When we see leadership failures, we should respond not with scandal-seeking but with prayer for restoration. The system assumes the leader will repent; the offering exists precisely to facilitate that return.

text_kjv: And he shall bring the bullock unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the LORD; and shall lay his hand upon the bullock's head, and kill the bullock before the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
The opening movements of the purification offering are identical to those of the burnt offering and fellowship offering: bring the animal to the tabernacle entrance, lay hand upon its head, slaughter it before the LORD. This continuity is important—all three systems share the same initial ritual. But the chata't diverges sharply after the slaughter. Whereas the burnt offering is wholly consumed on the altar and the fellowship offering is shared between God and the people at a meal, the blood of the priestly chata't will be brought inside the tabernacle itself (v5), anointing the veil and other inner sanctum objects. The slaughter location is 'before the LORD'—at the entrance to the sacred precinct, not inside it.

The hand-laying (semickhah) is the gesture of identification: the priest lays his hand on the bullock's head, symbolically transferring responsibility and sin to the animal. The animal becomes the substitute, receiving the consequence that the priest's sin has created. The slaughter then severs the animal from life, symbolizing the death-consequence of sin (Romans 6:23 will later frame this theologically: 'the wages of sin is death'). The priest personally performs this act (the priest 'shall...lay his hand...and kill')—not a servant or subordinate. Personal accountability is embodied in the gesture.

word_study.meaning: To bring, to carry, to lead. The basic movement of presenting the sacrificial animal to the sanctuary.
word_study.significance: The active verb emphasizes the offerer's role—the priest brings; he is not brought. This preserves personal agency even in confession. The sinner approaches; the remedy doesn't come to the sinner. This pattern underlies all repentance: the sinner must move toward God, not wait for automatic restoration.

word_study.meaning: The entrance of the tent of meeting. The threshold between the ordinary world and the sacred space.
word_study.significance: The door (pethach) is a threshold of separation. The animal is brought to the entrance; the bullock does not enter the inner space. However, its blood will (v5), showing that while the physical animal remains outside, its purifying power will penetrate to the innermost sanctum.

word_study.meaning: To lay, to place, to put one's hand upon the head. The verb samach means to lean upon, to support; in ritual context, to place the hand as an act of identification and transfer.
word_study.significance: This gesture (semikhah) is the critical moment of substitution. The priest's hand makes contact; the sin is transferred to the animal. Leviticus 1:4 (the burnt offering) uses the same gesture, but the theological significance differs. For the burnt offering, the gesture may signify the offerer's identification with the offering of devotion. For the chata't, it signifies the transfer of contamination. The animal becomes the bearer of the priest's sin-pollution.

word_study.meaning: To slaughter, to kill, to slay. The technical term for the ritual killing of a sacrificial animal.
word_study.significance: The slaughter is not killing for food; it is ritual death as the consequence of sin. The Covenant Rendering preserves this by using 'slaughter' rather than 'kill,' marking it as ceremonial action. This death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23); the animal pays the price that the priest's sin has incurred.

word_study.meaning: In the presence of the LORD, before the face of the LORD. Indicates that the action occurs in a sacred context, under God's witness and authority.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears repeatedly in sacrificial contexts (Leviticus 1:3, 3:1, 4:4, etc.) and establishes that every sacrifice is a divine-human encounter. God is not absent from the tabernacle; He witnesses the ritual. The slaughter is not merely human activity but an act performed in God's immediate presence.

cross_references.connection: The burnt offering uses the identical initial procedure: bring, lay hand, slaughter. This shows that multiple offerings share a common ritual introduction, but their purposes and subsequent procedures diverge.

Describes the Suffering Servant: 'the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all'—echoing the principle of semikhah (laying on of hands), where the priest's or people's sin is transferred to a substitute.

Paul frames sin's ultimate consequence as death: 'the wages of sin is death: but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.' The slaughter of the bullock dramatizes this theological principle.

For a poorer offerer unable to bring a bullock, a bird is permitted as a chata't, but the procedure includes wringing the neck 'at the door of the tabernacle'—showing that even simplified procedures preserve the threshold location and the death consequence.
Without shedding of blood is no remission of sins.' This verse encodes the principle enacted in Leviticus 4:4: the death of the substitute is the mechanism of purification.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern ritual, the slaughter of the sacrificial animal at the sanctuary entrance marked a transition point between ordinary and sacred space. The entrance (pethach) was itself sacred but accessible; the inner precinct was restricted. By slaughtering at the threshold, the priest enacted the consequence of sin at the place where profane and sacred meet. The hand-laying (semikhah) gesture appears in Mesopotamian rituals as well—the laying on of hands as a gesture of transfer. But in Israel's system, what is transferred is not just punishment but contamination: the animal receives the ritual pollution that sin has created, and the blood carries that pollution into the sanctuary for purification. This reflects Israel's distinctive theology—sin is not primarily punishable offense but ritual danger requiring decontamination.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:9 teaches that 'the law of Moses was a shadow of those things which were to come—namely, the coming of the Son of God.' The ritual of Leviticus 4:4—bring, lay hand, slaughter—is one such shadow, pointing to Christ's sacrificial death as the antitype. The laying on of hands in verse 4 foreshadows the laying on of hands in modern LDS ordination: in ancient times, hands transferred sin to an animal; in the Restoration, hands confer authority and blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6 teaches that 'the light which is in all things...giveth life to all things.' The death of the animal in verse 4 teaches the inverse principle: the penalty for violating God's law is death. This principle underlies D&C 29:41-43, where the Lord explains that death entered the world through Adam's transgression and remains the consequence of sin.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In modern temple worship, the laying on of hands is central to several ordinances: blessing, ordination, healing (D&C 42:48-50). The principle of placing hands on another's head as a gesture of transfer—whether transferring sin (Leviticus 4:4) or conferring blessing (D&C 35:20)—runs throughout covenant practice. Both old and new covenant recognize that the gesture carries spiritual weight.

commentary.christological_typology: The hand-laying on the bullock's head in verse 4 is one of the clearest typological images of Christ's substitutionary work. The sinner transfers his contamination to the innocent animal; the animal dies instead of the sinner. John the Baptist's declaration in John 1:29—'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world'—directly applies this typology. Christ is the ultimate Sacrifice in whom the sinner's hand (sin) is placed, and who bears away the consequence. Hebrews 10:10 teaches that 'we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.' The animal's slaughter foreshadows Christ's death as the once-and-for-all purification.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that repentance requires the sinner's active participation. The priest brings the animal; he lays his hand upon it; he performs the slaughter. These are not passive acts done to him but actions he initiates and completes. In modern repentance, we similarly take active steps: we confess to God and to proper authorities; we make restitution; we commit to change. The repentance process is something we do, not something done to us. The ritual also teaches substitution: the animal bears the price so the sinner is freed. In learning to repent and accept the Atonement, we recognize that Christ bears the price of our sin so we can be free. And like the priest, we must bring ourselves to the boundary—confessing at the door of the tabernacle (metaphorically, in confession to God and priesthood leaders)—before purification can occur.

text_kjv: And the priest that is anointed shall take of the bullock's blood, and bring it to the tabernacle of the congregation:

commentary.narrative:
Here the priestly chata't diverges radically from other sacrifices. The blood enters the tabernacle—inside the sacred precinct where only the priest is permitted. This is the crucial moment. Whereas the blood of the burnt offering and fellowship offering is applied to the outer altar (in front of the tabernacle), the blood of the priestly chata't penetrates into the tent of meeting itself. This difference reflects the severity of the priestly sin: when the high priest sins, the contamination reaches into the inner sanctuary, and the purification must therefore follow the contamination inward.

The priest 'takes' of the blood—not all the blood (which may be poured out at the base of the outer altar, as verse 7 suggests), but some of it, enough for sprinkling. This section of blood becomes the tool of purification, carried into the sacred space by the priest's hand. The movement is inward, penetrating, reaching deeper than ordinary sacrificial procedure. Later in verse 6, this blood will be sprinkled 'seven times before the LORD...before the veil of the sanctuary,' reaching to the boundary of the most holy place. The spatial logic is clear: sin contamination follows a path; blood purification must follow the same path inward, to the source.

word_study.meaning: To take, to receive, to seize. In ritual context, to take possession of something for a designated purpose.
word_study.significance: The priest actively takes the blood—this is not passive sprinkling by an assistant. The high priest personally engages with the medium of purification. The verb implies agency and intentional action toward restoration.

word_study.meaning: Blood. In sacrificial theology, the vehicle of life-force and purification. 'The life of the flesh is in the blood' (Leviticus 17:11).
word_study.significance: Blood in Levitical theology is not merely iron oxide and proteins—it is the life-force (nefesh) of the animal, now available for purification. The Covenant Rendering and traditional understanding recognize that blood represents life itself, and the life of the substitute cleanses the sanctuary of contamination.

word_study.meaning: To bring, to carry, to lead. Same verb as in verse 4, now applied to the blood.
word_study.significance: The priest carries the blood into the sacred space. This is not automatic; the priest must transport it. The action emphasizes that purification is achieved through deliberate, ritual movement. Contamination spread; purification must be deliberately applied where contamination has reached.

word_study.meaning: The tent of meeting. The tabernacle structure where God's presence dwells and where Israel meets God through priestly mediation.
word_study.significance: This is the sanctuary interior, the holy place. Unlike verse 4 ('the door of the tabernacle'), which is the threshold, verse 5 specifies entrance to the tabernacle itself. The blood crosses the threshold and enters the inner space. This inward movement is what distinguishes the priestly chata't from other offerings and marks it as addressing a deeper level of contamination.

cross_references.connection: Provides instructions to the priest about handling chata't blood and explains that the meat of the chata't is holy and must be eaten by the priests in a holy place, showing that the chata't involves the priest at multiple points—not just presenting the animal but processing the blood and consuming the meat.

The foundational statement: 'The life of the flesh is in the blood...and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls.' This verse explains why blood is the instrument of purification—it carries life-force that can undo death-contamination.

Describes Christ's priestly work: 'Now of the things we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens...a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man.' Christ's blood enters the heavenly sanctuary, as the priestly chata't blood entered the earthly tabernacle.

Describes what happens to the bullock's body: it is taken outside the camp and burned in the ashes. The blood is taken inward (verse 5); the carcass is taken outward. This shows the complete disposal system: the source of purification goes to the inner sanctuary; the source of contamination goes outside the camp.
The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin'—applying the principle of Leviticus 4:5 (blood cleanses) to Christ's blood, which enters the heavenly tabernacle and cleanses believers.

commentary.historical_context: The tabernacle's interior geography reinforced theological hierarchy in ancient Israel. The outer courtyard was accessible to lay worshippers; the holy place was restricted to priests; the most holy place was restricted to the high priest alone on Yom Kippur. By permitting blood to enter the inner sanctum only in the case of priestly sin, the system physically enacted the principle that priestly sin reaches deeper into the sacred than lay sin. The inward movement of blood followed the presumed inward path of contamination. Ancient temples in other cultures maintained similar spatial hierarchies, but Israel's distinctive feature was making the spatial movement of the purifying blood visible and intentional. The priest becomes the vehicle of purification, carrying the life-force inward to neutralize the death-contamination outward.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 11:11 records the Risen Lord bearing His wounds and showing that His blood was 'spilt for the remission of the sins of the world.' The principle of blood entering the sanctuary (Leviticus 4:5) is fulfilled when Christ's blood enters the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8-9), accomplishing the type's ultimate purpose.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:40-42 speaks of those who enter the celestial kingdom as 'made perfect through Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, who wrought out this perfect atonement through the shedding of his own blood.' The shedding and application of blood in Leviticus 4:5 foreshadows the Atonement's application in the heavenly sanctuary.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Modern temple ordinances involve the application of symbolic oil and water, fulfilling and transcending the old covenant's use of blood. The sacred space of the temple—with its inner chambers and restricted access—maintains the tabernacle's structural hierarchy. The principle that deeper access requires greater righteousness and more elaborate purification remains embedded in temple practice.

commentary.christological_typology: The blood entering the sanctuary in Leviticus 4:5 is a precise typological preview of Hebrews 9:11-12: 'But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle...by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.' Christ's blood does what the chata't blood only partially and temporarily accomplished—it enters the heavenly sanctuary and provides complete, eternal purification. The movement inward in verse 5 prefigures Christ's ascension into heaven, where His blood performs its eternal purifying function before God.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that when we seek repentance and purification, the remedy reaches into the depths where contamination has penetrated. Confession to a priesthood holder (the modern equivalent of the priest in verse 5) means that someone with authority carries our repentance into the sacred precincts of the Church—our sins are not just between us and God but involve the broader community's sanctity. This is why confession to priesthood authority matters: the priest-leader brings the matter into the sanctuary of God's house, where it can be properly addressed at the deepest level. For those in priesthood positions, it teaches that you carry a solemn responsibility—you are the vessel through which purification reaches the sanctuary. For all members, it reminds us that repentance is not merely private sentiment but involves bringing our broken covenant-selves to the priest and allowing the institution and the leader to participate in our purification.

text_kjv: And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the LORD, before the vail of the sanctuary.

commentary.narrative:
The priest dips his finger into the blood and performs a precise, controlled ritual action: seven sprinklings before the LORD, directed at the veil of the sanctuary. This is the climax of the priestly chata't procedure. Seven is the biblical number of completeness and perfection; seven sprinklings ensure thorough, exhaustive purification. The veil (parokhet) is the curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place—the boundary of God's innermost dwelling. When the high priest sins, the contamination is understood to threaten that sacred boundary. The blood must reach that boundary to purify it.

Note the technique: dipping the finger, not pouring. The verb hizzah (sprinkle) produces a fine spray, directed precisely. This differs from zaraq ('dash'), used for the blood of burnt and fellowship offerings on the outer altar. The distinction is deliberate: the outer altar receives a vigorous dashing of blood; the inner sanctuary receives a careful sprinkling applied with the finger. The intimacy and precision of the gesture matches the sacred space's holiness. The priest stands before the veil, finger-dipped in the blood of the substitute, and restores the boundary that the priestly sin has contaminated. The action is priestly privilege and responsibility combined—only the priest can perform this; the priest must perform this.

word_study.meaning: To dip, to immerse partially. The finger enters the blood, absorbs it, and emerges with the purifying substance adhering.
word_study.significance: Dipping (rather than pouring) suggests a measured, controlled action. The priest takes exactly what the finger can carry. This is not profligacy but precision—the exact amount needed for the ritual is taken, no more.

word_study.meaning: To sprinkle, to scatter in fine drops. A technique that differs from zaraq ('to dash' or 'to splash'), producing a controlled spray.
word_study.significance: Hizzah appears in chata't contexts; zaraq appears in burnt offering contexts. The distinction is technical but theologically significant. The outer altar's burnt offerings receive the vigorous dashing (zaraq); the inner sanctuary's purification receives the careful sprinkling (hizzah). The Covenant Rendering preserves this distinction by translating hizzah specifically as 'sprinkle' to mark its difference from 'dashing.'

word_study.meaning: Seven times. Sheva (seven) + pe'amim (times/occasions). Seven is the biblical number of completeness, covenant, and holiness (the Sabbath is the seventh day; seventy years end a jubilee).
word_study.significance: Seven sprinklings are not arbitrary. The number signifies that the purification is complete and exhaustive. This is not perfunctory or partial; seven ensures thoroughness. The Covenant Rendering's note emphasizes that seven applications demonstrate complete cleansing of the boundary.

word_study.meaning: In the presence of, before the face of. The action occurs in God's immediate awareness.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears five times in the chata't opening procedures (verses 3, 4, 6, 7, and implicitly throughout). The constant refrain—'before the LORD'—establishes that no part of the purification ritual occurs outside God's presence or without God's witness. The priest is not performing magic; he is performing a divinely authorized ritual in God's presence for God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: The curtain or veil separating the holy place from the most holy place. A physical barrier woven from fine linen with cherubim (Exodus 26:31).
word_study.significance: The veil (parokhet) is not merely decorative; it represents the boundary between the accessible holy place and the inaccessible holy of holies. When the high priest sins, the contamination is understood to threaten this boundary. The blood must reach the veil to purify it. In Matthew 27:51, Mark 15:38, and Luke 23:45, the veil tears at Jesus' death—the ultimate fulfillment and transcendence of this purification principle. Christ's death makes the veil unnecessary; believers now have direct access (Hebrews 10:19-22).

word_study.meaning: Holiness, sanctity, the holy place. Qodesh in Leviticus can refer to the entire sanctum or specifically to the holy place (as opposed to the holy of holies).
word_study.significance: The full phrase 'the veil of the sanctuary' (parokhet haqodesh) locates the veil within the sacred precinct. The sanctuary is holy, and its boundary (the veil) must be preserved in holiness. The blood's application to the veil maintains the sanctity that priestly sin has threatened.

cross_references.connection: Applies the same sprinkling procedure (seven times before the veil) for the congregation's chata't. This shows that regardless of the offerer's status, the severity of the contamination determines the depth of the purification—contamination in the sanctuary requires internal blood application.

Interprets the old covenant purification: 'Almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission...It was therefore necessary that the patterns of things in the heavens should be purified with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.'

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest sprinkles the blood of the bullock toward the mercy seat (kapporet, the lid of the ark) and the blood of the goat for the people. Yom Kippur expands and intensifies what Leviticus 4:6 initiates—the penetration of blood into the most holy spaces.

Jesus' death coincides with the tearing of the temple veil (parokhet), suggesting that Christ's sacrificial death makes the old covenant's veil-boundaries obsolete. Christ's blood cleanses definitively where the chata't blood only provisionally cleansed.

Explains the significance of the veil's tearing: 'Having...boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus...and having an high priest over the house of God...let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.' Christ's Atonement removes the veil-barrier that Levitical purification could only temporarily maintain.

commentary.historical_context: The physical layout of the tabernacle—outer courtyard, holy place, most holy place—created concentric circles of holiness, with access corresponding to ritual status. Only the high priest could approach the veil; only he could perform this sprinkling. The technique of blood application (dipping the finger, precise sprinkling, seven times) reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that ritual precision mattered. Blood was not casually applied; it was carefully targeted at the specific boundary where contamination had reached. The seven sprinklings are a complete number in several ancient traditions, but they are especially characteristic of Israelite covenant ritual (e.g., the seven circuits of Jericho, Joshua 6:15). The practice shows theological sophistication: the more sacred the space, the more precise the purification; the deeper the contamination, the more elaborate the remedy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 9:7-8 teaches that the law of Moses 'was spiritual...And there were strict commandments given unto the children of Israel, that they should observe these things.' The seven sprinklings of Leviticus 4:6 exemplify those strict commandments—the ritual precision required for maintaining covenant holiness. The Book of Mormon recognizes that the law of Moses, while preparatory, demanded exact obedience to its particulars.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:74-75 specifies that ordinations in the Church must be performed by one 'that is ordained...that he may know he hath authority.' Similarly, Leviticus 4:6 specifies that the anointed priest (authorized) must perform the sprinkling. Authority in covenant practice is not generic; it is specific, particular, and exercised in precise ways. D&C 1:38 teaches that 'whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same'—establishing that God's authority matters more than the vehicle, but both must be legitimate.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple ordinances involve precise gestures and actions performed by authorized individuals. The laying on of hands, the anointing with oil, the specific words and movements—all parallel the principle that Leviticus 4:6 embodies: spiritual efficacy flows through authorized, precise, deliberate ritual action. Modern temple practice preserves the ancient understanding that holiness is not achieved through sincere intention alone but through faithful performance of covenant ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: The seven sprinklings of blood before the veil in Leviticus 4:6 foreshadow Christ's once-and-for-all entry into the heavenly sanctuary. Hebrews 9:24-26 develops this explicitly: 'For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us...Nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest entereth into the holy place every year with blood of others; For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.' The repeated sprinklings of the old covenant chata't are completed in Christ's single, perfect entry and offering. The veil that separated God's presence becomes unnecessary; Christ's blood opens the way.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us that purification of our deepest places requires the most careful, deliberate action. Casual repentance doesn't reach deep contamination. The priest's seven-fold sprinkling before the veil models the thoroughness required when we allow sin to penetrate to the core of our covenant relationship with God. When we confess, we must confess fully and completely, not glossing over areas where contamination has reached deepest. For those in leadership, it teaches that purification ceremonies (setting apart, ordinations, excommunication, rebaptism) must be performed with full authority, precise understanding, and complete seriousness—they are not administrative procedures but sacred rituals that restore sanctity. For all members, it reminds us that our relationship with God requires tending—like the veil that must be purified, our covenant standing requires regular, deliberate attention to maintain holiness. The seven sprinklings suggest that restoration is not instant but requires sustained, focused action.

text_kjv: And if the whole congregation of Israel sin through ignorance, and the thing be hid from the eyes of the assembly, and they have done somewhat against any of the commandments of the LORD concerning things which should not be done, and are guilty;

commentary.narrative:
Leviticus 4:13 introduces the second category of the purification offering (chata't): unintentional sin committed by the entire congregation of Israel. This is a profound shift from the individual cases in verses 2–12. The text acknowledges a theological reality that ancient Israel had to confront: communities, not just individuals, can fall into transgression. The mechanism is strikingly specific: the sin must be hidden from the eyes of the assembly—meaning the community as a whole remains ignorant of their violation. This is not deliberate defiance but rather a collective oversight, possibly arising from a misunderstanding of the law propagated by leadership or a communal error in interpretation.

The phrase "the thing be hid from the eyes of the assembly" (ne'elam davar me'einei haqqahal) is the operational trigger. It establishes that ignorance, not intent, defines the category. The congregation commits an act forbidden by the Lord's commandments—"things which should not be done"—but without awareness of transgression. This condition of hiddeness is essential: once the sin becomes known (as verse 14 will show), the community enters a new phase of responsibility and required atonement. The final phrase "and are guilty" (ve'ashemu) indicates that guilt attaches automatically upon transgression, regardless of knowledge. In Israel's theology, violation of divine law incurs objective guilt that requires purification, not merely subjective awareness of wrongdoing.
commentary.narrative_continued: What makes this verse revolutionary in ancient Near Eastern religion is the principle that a nation can sin corporately and require corporate purification. Unlike pagan systems focused on individual piety and divination, Israel's covenant framework holds the entire people responsible for maintaining holiness. The gravity of this category is immediately evident: the congregation's unintentional sin will require the same offering as the high priest's sin (verses 3–12)—a young bull, the costliest animal in the prescribed scale. This equality of offering between priestly and communal failure sends a theological message: collective sin against God's law is as serious as the sin of the one who mediates between God and the people. The assembly's failure to know, understand, and obey the law represents a fundamental breakdown in the community's capacity to remain holy before the Lord.

word_study.meaning: An organized gathering or assembly; in covenant context, the entire assembled people as a corporate body. The term emphasizes collectivity and formal corporate identity, not merely a gathering of individuals.
word_study.significance: The use of adat (congregation/community) rather than am (people) underscores the formal, organized structure of Israel's corporate covenant relationship with the Lord. The congregation is a juridical and liturgical entity that can incur guilt as a body and bear responsibility before God.

word_study.meaning: To go astray, wander, or err; to sin through ignorance or inadvertence. The root implies unintentional deviation from the correct path, not deliberate rebellion.
word_study.significance: Shagah establishes the psychological and moral category: this sin belongs to the realm of error, not willful transgression. The Levitical system recognizes degrees of culpability—unintentional sin is a distinct legal category from presumptuous sin (Numbers 15:30–31). This distinction reflects biblical anthropology: humans are fallible and prone to unintentional error; the sacrificial system provides remedy for such failures without requiring execution or permanent estrangement from God.

word_study.meaning: To be hidden, concealed, or kept secret; to escape notice or awareness. The passive voice indicates that the matter remains beyond the community's collective perception.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering (TCR) preserves the nuance: 'the matter being hidden from the eyes of the assembly.' This emphasizes epistemic ignorance—the community genuinely does not know. The condition is not that individual members are unaware (some might know), but that the collective assembly, operating as a corporate entity through its leadership, has not recognized the violation. This raises the question of corporate moral knowledge: when does a community know something? The answer shapes how and when purification becomes necessary.

word_study.meaning: Commandments, precepts, or divine instructions. Mitzvah literally means 'that which is commanded' and refers to the totality of God's revealed will.
word_study.significance: The congregation's sin is against the mitzvot—the corpus of divine law revealed to Israel at Sinai. This establishes that the purification offering addresses violations of God's explicit covenant stipulations, not merely moral intuitions or customary practices. The congregation's role is to know, remember, and obey these commandments collectively.

word_study.meaning: To be guilty, to bear guilt, or to incur liability. The root asham conveys both the state of guilt and the obligation to make restitution or atonement.
word_study.significance: Ashem establishes that guilt is not a subjective feeling but an objective state. The congregation becomes liable (ashmim) through the act of transgression itself, independent of awareness. Guilt here is covenantal status: the people have violated the terms of their agreement with the Lord and must undergo purification to restore right standing. The acknowledgment 'and are guilty' marks the transition from ignorance to accountability.

cross_references.connection: Introduces the general category of unintentional sin (shagah) that triggers the purification offering for individuals; verse 13 extends this principle to the entire congregation.

Addresses communal unintentional sin and specifies that when the entire congregation sins unknowingly, they shall offer a bull for a purification offering and a ram for a burnt offering, with the procedure similar to Leviticus 4:13–21.

NT reflection on sin, guilt, and the necessity of confession; the principle that guilt exists objectively before God, regardless of human awareness, parallels the Levitical concept that ashem (guilt) attaches automatically upon violation.

The Lord's statement that those who sin against the knowledge given to them shall be judged according to their works; echoes the Levitical principle that the congregation's corporate responsibility is measured by the mitzvot (commandments) they have received.

Declares that God knows all things and nothing is hidden from Him; contrasts with the congregation's ignorance in this verse and establishes that what is 'hidden from the eyes of the assembly' is fully known to God.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, the mechanism for collective decision-making and knowledge dissemination flowed through the elders and priestly leadership. When the entire congregation sinned through ignorance, it typically meant that misinterpretation or miscommunication of the law had propagated through the community's leadership structures. For example, if the priestly teachers incorrectly interpreted a commandment concerning a festival observance or dietary law, and the people followed this misinterpretation en masse, the entire community would incur guilt—even though no deliberate defiance had occurred. The requirement for a young bull (the costliest offering in the scale of Leviticus 5) indicates that such communal sin was regarded as extremely serious, more severe than individual sin by ordinary people but equivalent to the high priest's sin. This reflects the principle that the community's corporate holiness was essential to the ongoing viability of the covenant relationship. A nation that systematically errs in understanding God's law places itself in grave jeopardy before the sanctuary, and remediation requires the most costly sacrifice. The ancient Near Eastern context (Egypt, Mesopotamia) had no exact parallel to this concept of corporate sin requiring collective atonement; Israelite covenant theology stands unique in its recognition of communal culpability and collective purification.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon reflects similar theology of corporate sin and covenant breaking. In Mosiah 2:32–33, King Benjamin teaches that when people collectively break covenant they bring condemnation upon the whole nation. Alma 9:23–24 illustrates how the Nephites' corporate rejection of prophetic warnings led to collective judgment. The principle that unintentional sin by a community still requires atonement parallels Levitical theology: the Nephites at times sinned through ignorance or misunderstanding of God's laws and required collective repentance and sacrifice. The chata't offering's requirement for the community's leadership (elders) to lay hands on the animal parallels the corporate nature of covenant responsibility in Book of Mormon society.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:30 defines the Church as the 'only true and living church' contingent upon its keeping of covenants. D&C 82:3–4 teaches that 'whatsoever you have received [by revelation], you are bound to keep; and whoso breaketh this covenant, after he hath received it, and altogether turneth therefrom, shall not have forgiveness of sins in this world nor in the world to come.' This establishes that corporate bodies (like Israel in Leviticus 4:13) incur guilt when they collectively depart from received covenants. The purification offering imagery in Levitical sacrifice is fulfilled in Christ's atonement; modern covenant communities gain access to that atonement through repentance and obedience to revealed truth (D&C 58:42–43).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The chata't offering was brought to the tabernacle (later the temple), where the priest performed the purification ritual in the sanctuary itself. This foreshadows how the Church functions as a covenant community seeking to remain pure before God. The laying on of hands by the elders in verse 15 parallels the role of priesthood leadership in modern temples, where elders and authorized servants represent the community in sacred ordinances. The principle that corporate sin requires corporate ritual acknowledgment and purification continues in modern temple worship, where the community gathers to renew covenants and seek sanctification as a corporate body.

commentary.christological_typology: The congregation's unintentional sin requiring a young bull for purification prefigures the necessity of Christ's atoning sacrifice for all humanity. Jesus Christ, like the prescribed bull, was without blemish and offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The congregation's ignorance of their transgression parallels humanity's condition before the full revelation of Christ: people transgressed divine law without fully understanding the cosmic consequences of sin. Christ's purification offering addresses not only individual violations but the collective sin of humankind—the corporate transgression of the entire race. The Levitical principle that objective guilt attaches to transgression regardless of subjective awareness finds its answer in Christ's atonement: His blood purifies both those who knowingly and unknowingly violated God's law, making one comprehensive sacrifice for the sins of all (1 John 2:2).
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, Latter-day Saints recognize that congregations (wards, stakes, the Church as a whole) can fall into corporate error or sin through misunderstanding of divine law or failure of leadership to properly transmit covenant principles. Just as ancient Israel required corporate repentance when the assembly sinned unintentionally, modern communities of saints benefit from collective acknowledgment of mistakes and recommitment to revealed truth. When a congregation recognizes it has strayed—through incomplete understanding of doctrine, cultural accommodation, or leadership oversight—the pathway to restoration involves corporate confession, renewed study of foundational principles (the modern equivalent of rediscovering the law), and collective recommitment to covenant. Members should not assume that because they personally did not intend to transgress, the community bears no responsibility. The Levitical principle affirms that corporate entities are morally accountable before God. This should motivate members to support their leaders in correctly understanding and teaching gospel principles, to speak up when error is suspected, and to participate in the community's ongoing repentance and renewal.

text_kjv: When the sin, which they have sinned against it, is known, then the congregation shall offer a young bullock for the sin, and bring him before the tabernacle of the congregation.

commentary.narrative: Verse 14 marks the decisive moment: the transition from hidden sin to known sin, from potential guilt to actual purification obligation. The phrase "when the sin...is known" (ki yinod'ah hachata't) indicates that awareness by the community triggers the sacrificial response. This is not punitive in character; rather, it is remedial. Once the congregation collectively recognizes that they have violated one of the Lord's commandments, the path forward is unmistakable: they must bring a young bull to the tabernacle as a purification offering. The cattle animal (young bullock, par ben-baqar) is the same offering required for the high priest's sin (verse 3), establishing a radical theological principle: the failure of the entire people to maintain covenant holiness is equivalent in gravity to the failure of the priest who stands between them and God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb yinod'ah ("is known") is passive, emphasizing that knowledge simply emerges—it is revealed, discovered, or recognized—rather than deliberately communicated or investigated. The assembly comes to understand their violation through instruction, observation, or the elders' recognition. Once this knowledge exists, there is no option for delay or alternative remedy: the congregation "shall offer" (v'hiqrivu haqqahal, with the collective subject acting in unity). The language of bringing the bull "before the tabernacle of the congregation" emphasizes the public, official nature of the remediation. This is not a private or hidden atonement but a visible, corporate act of the entire assembly acknowledging their failure and seeking restoration. The congregation, represented by its elders, brings the animal to the entrance of the tent of meeting—the liminal space between the secular and the sacred—initiating the purification procedure that will penetrate to the heart of the sanctuary.

word_study.meaning: Becomes known, is revealed, or comes to be perceived. The passive form indicates that knowledge arises through some discovery process, not through deliberate investigation or judicial finding.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'when the sin they have committed becomes known,' capturing the sense that knowledge emerges as a state-change, not a moment of deliberate judgment. For the congregation, the transition from ignorance to knowledge is the hinge-point that activates obligation. This reflects Israelite legal theory: culpability becomes actionable when the violation enters collective awareness. The congregation did not sin by failing to know; they sinned through the transgression itself. But the knowledge of the sin is what triggers the remedial obligation.

word_study.meaning: To bring near, to present, or to offer. In sacrificial context, to present an animal offering to the Lord at the sanctuary.
word_study.significance: Qarab emphasizes the spatial and relational act of bringing something into proximity with God. The congregation does not merely pay a fine or perform a public confession; they actively bring the animal to the sanctuary, drawing it near to the Lord's presence. This is the congregation's participation in the purification process—a physical enactment of their desire to draw near again to God's presence after having transgressed.

word_study.meaning: A young bull, specifically a bovine animal in the prime of its strength (typically 2-3 years old), from the baqar (cattle herd). Distinguished from 'egel (calf) and mature ox.
word_study.significance: The young bull is the most valuable sacrificial animal in the prescribed scale of Leviticus 5:14–6:7. Its costliness reflects the seriousness of the transgression. That the congregation must offer this same animal as the high priest (Leviticus 4:3) indicates that communal sin against God's law is weighted equally with priestly sin in terms of its contaminating power. The value of the offering corresponds to the gravity of the transgression, not the status of the offerer.

word_study.meaning: The tent of meeting; the portable sanctuary where the Lord's presence dwells and where priests perform the sacrificial service. Ohel (tent) emphasizes the temporary, portable structure; mo'ed (meeting/appointment) emphasizes it as the place where Israel is appointed to meet with God.
word_study.significance: The tabernacle is the intersection between the human and divine realms, the place where atonement is mediated and purification is accomplished. By bringing the bull before the ohel mo'ed, the congregation is positioning themselves at the threshold of God's presence, acknowledging their need for purification and their dependent relationship on the Lord.

cross_references.connection: The high priest's purification offering also requires a young bull (par ben-baqar), establishing the equivalence between priestly and communal sin in terms of sacrificial obligation.

Details the laying on of hands and presentation of an animal before the Lord; the congregation in verse 14 follows this same template of drawing near and presenting an offering at the sanctuary entrance.

Provides parallel legislation for communal unintentional sin, specifying that when the whole congregation sins unknowingly, one bull shall be offered for a purification offering with the same procedure outlined in Leviticus 4.

Records how Ezra and the Levites 'read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense'; illustrates the mechanism by which a community comes to know (nod'ah) whether it has transgressed the law—through public instruction and clarification of the commandments.

Paul's teaching that the body of Christ is one organism with many members; reflects the principle of corporate identity and corporate responsibility that underlies the congregation's collective obligation in Leviticus 4:14.

commentary.historical_context: The tabernacle (ohel mo'ed) was the portable sanctuary that accompanied Israel through the wilderness and eventually was replicated in the temple at Jerusalem. The phrase 'tabernacle of the congregation' emphasizes that this is a communal structure, the gathering place for the entire assembly. In ancient Israel, when a community came to the sanctuary with an offering, it was a public event witnessed by other worshippers and the priestly establishment. The requirement that the congregation bring their sin offering openly, before the entire community, served social and theological functions: it publicly acknowledged the failure, it reinforced the community's dependence on God, and it demonstrated that even the collective Israel stood under judgment and required atonement. The procedure in verse 14 does not specify how the congregation decides to bring the bull—was it a formal assembly decision? Did the elders determine the moment? The text's silence suggests that once knowledge becomes widespread, the obligation is self-evident and automatic. This reflects a society with strong internal covenant consciousness: when the law is violated and the fact becomes known, immediate remedial action is expected, without requiring elaborate judicial procedures or external compulsion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 46, Moroni raises the standard of liberty when the Nephites collectively drift from covenant. The people's recognition of their error (nod'ah)—that they are about to be destroyed through covenant-breaking—triggers immediate communal action toward repentance and restoration. Similarly, in Helaman 4:21–22, when the Nephites become aware (nod'ah, in principle) of their transgression and resulting military defeats, they seek to return to the Lord, essentially bringing their corporate 'offering' of repentance. The Book of Mormon consistently shows that awareness of sin is the prerequisite for remedial action; mere transgression without knowledge does not trigger the same level of obligation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:42–43 establishes that 'by this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.' The congregation in Leviticus 4:14 manifests repentance by confessing their sin (brought to light by knowledge) and immediately seeking to forsake it through the purification offering. D&C 64:7 teaches that God has forgiven your sins, 'but ye are not forgiven of your sins until ye forgive one another'—implying that corporate bodies, like ancient Israel, must move together toward acknowledgment and remediation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The congregation's presentation of the bull before the tent of meeting parallels modern temple covenants, where the community of saints collectively covenant to live by God's law and maintain holiness. When members become aware that they or the broader Church community have strayed from covenant principles, the remedy mirrors Leviticus 4:14: renewed engagement with the temple, public confession of error (as appropriate), and collective recommitment to the law of God. The temple serves as the ohel mo'ed for modern Israel—the place where the community gathers to renew covenants and seek purification.

commentary.christological_typology: The congregation's knowledge of their sin and immediate presentation of a purification offering foreshadows humanity's eventual recognition of corporate guilt before God and the necessity of Christ's atoning sacrifice. When knowledge of sin becomes undeniable—when the veil is lifted and humanity recognizes its collective transgression—the only remedy is the perfect offering, Christ Himself. Hebrews 10:1–4 teaches that the old sacrifices could not perfect those who drew near, but Christ's one offering 'for ever' (Hebrews 10:12) purifies the conscience. The transition from hidden sin to known sin in verse 13–14 parallels the spiritual awakening that leads souls to Christ: the recognition of transgression is the prerequisite for seeking atonement through Him.
commentary.application: Modern Church members should recognize that knowledge of error activates obligation. When a member, family, or congregation becomes aware that they have drifted from gospel principles—whether through misunderstanding, cultural drift, or institutional inertia—the Levitical principle of nod'ah applies: knowledge creates immediate responsibility to seek remedy. Members should not delay in recommitting to covenants once error is recognized. Furthermore, leaders bear special responsibility for ensuring that the congregation comes to know God's law correctly. Just as ancient Israel's sin often arose from misinterpretation propagated by leadership, modern leaders must take care to teach doctrine clearly and to correct misunderstandings when they emerge. When the community becomes aware of institutional error, the appropriate response is not defensiveness but immediate remedial action—analogous to bringing the bull to the tabernacle. This requires humility, transparency, and collective commitment to realigning with revealed truth. Individual members can apply this principle in their personal lives: the moment you become aware of a transgression, that knowledge creates the obligation to seek atonement through repentance and recommitment to covenant.

text_kjv: And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands upon the head of the bullock before the LORD: and the bullock shall be killed before the LORD.

commentary.narrative: Verse 15 introduces the crucial ritual of semikhah—the laying on of hands—performed by the elders of the congregation on the head of the bull. This act is far more than a mere procedural gesture; it is the mechanism of identification and substitution that lies at the heart of Levitical purification theology. The elders (ziqnei ha'edah), who represent the congregation's corporate identity and bear responsibility for the community's instruction in divine law, place their hands on the animal, transferring the community's guilt and identity to the bull. This is a remarkably physical theology: the people's transgression is made tangible through the contact of human hands with the animal's head. The multiple hands of multiple elders on a single animal emphasize the unified corporate nature of the congregation's sin and atonement. The congregation does not bring multiple animals, one per family or tribe; they bring one bull and collectively identify with it through their representatives.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second clause—"and the bullock shall be killed before the LORD"—follows inevitably upon the semikhah. The slaughter is not specified as to who performs it (priest, elder, or designated individual), but it occurs "before the LORD," in the sacred space, witnessed by the assembled community or at minimum the priestly officials. The killing of the bull, once the elders have laid hands upon it, represents the death of the congregation's guilt—a vicarious death where the innocent animal bears the consequence that, by right, the transgressing people should bear. This principle will be reinforced in verse 16–18 when the blood is brought into the sanctuary and applied to the altars. The theology here is not one of human sacrifice (which was abhorrent to Israelite covenant law, in contrast to some surrounding cultures) but of vicarious animal sacrifice as a substitute. The congregation remains alive and reconciled; the bull dies in their stead.

word_study.meaning: Elders; the senior or leading men of the community, typically those with age, wisdom, and institutional authority. In Israel, elders served judicial, administrative, and representative functions.
word_study.significance: The elders are not merely participants in the offering; they are representatives of the congregation before God. By laying their hands on the bull, they act as surrogates for the entire assembly, enacting the community's identification with the sacrifice. This role reflects the elders' responsibility for the congregation's spiritual welfare and their capacity to speak and act on behalf of the people. The fact that multiple elders perform semikhah together (the plural 'elders' implies more than one) emphasizes that this is a corporate act, not an individual gesture.

word_study.transliteration: samakh (from samakh, 'to lean upon' or 'to support')
word_study.meaning: To lay hands on, to place hands upon, or to lean/press. In sacrificial context, semikhah denotes the ritual placement of the offerer's hand(s) on the animal's head, symbolizing identification and the transfer of the offerer's status or guilt to the animal.
word_study.significance: Semikhah (hand-laying) is the foundational ritual act that binds the offerer to the sacrifice. It is not magical but covenantal: through physical contact, the person identifies with the animal and, in the context of a purification offering, transfers their guilt to a substitute. The act presupposes a theology of representation and substitution that is central to all Levitical sacrifice. Semikhah creates the nexus between the human transgressor and the innocent victim. In later Jewish tradition, this became central to the understanding of the Day of Atonement, where the high priest lays hands on the scapegoat to transfer the sins of Israel (Leviticus 16:21).

word_study.meaning: A young bull or bullock, specifically a male bovine in its prime (2-3 years old). Distinguished from calf (egel) and older ox.
word_study.significance: The par is the most valuable animal in the sacrificial scale and is reserved for the most serious transgressions (high priest and congregation). Its strength and vigor make it a fitting substitute—not a weakling or defective animal, but the community's most precious possession, offered to the Lord. The choice of the par (rather than a smaller animal) reflects the community's acknowledgment of the gravity of their transgression.

word_study.meaning: To slaughter, to cut the throat, or to kill (in the context of sacrifice). Shachat denotes the ritual killing that must be performed according to prescribed method (cutting the throat with a sharp blade to cause rapid blood loss).
word_study.significance: Shachat marks the moment of substitutionary death. The animal's death is not presented as cruel or tragic but as necessary and redemptive. The blood that flows from the shachat is the life-force (nefesh) that makes atonement (Leviticus 17:11). The passive voice 'shall be killed' in the KJV leaves the agent unspecified, but the principle is clear: death is enacted, the covenant rupture is addressed through the animal's demise.

word_study.meaning: In the presence of, before, or in the sight of the Lord. Emphasizes that the action occurs in God's presence, in sacred space or before the altar where God's presence is localized.
word_study.significance: The repeated phrase 'before the LORD' in verses 15, 16, and 17 establishes that the purification of the congregation occurs within the sacred geography of the sanctuary. This is not a private or secular matter but a covenantal transaction executed in the presence of God. The community's sin and atonement are transparently before the Lord; nothing is hidden in the purification process, even though the sin itself was initially hidden from the assembly's awareness.

cross_references.connection: The burnt offering also begins with the offerer laying hands on the animal's head before the Lord; semikhah is the foundational ritual act that binds offerer to offering across all sacrifice types.

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest lays both his hands on the scapegoat's head and confesses the sins of Israel, transferring all transgression to the animal; this is the fullest expression of semikhah as guilt-transfer.

Joshua receives authority as Moses' successor through the laying on of hands by Moses before the assembly; demonstrates that semikhah communicates identification, authority, and representative office.

The Suffering Servant passage describes how 'the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all'; directly echoes the Levitical mechanism of transferring guilt to a substitute through the laying on of hands.
Christ 'bare our sins in his own body on the tree'; applies the Levitical principle of substitutionary atonement (culminated in semikhah and slaughter) to Christ's redemptive work.

commentary.historical_context: The laying on of hands (semikhah) was a widespread gesture in the ancient Near East, used to signify authority, blessing, and transfer of responsibility. However, its use in the context of Israelite sacrifice appears to be distinctive—a ritual mechanism that articulates a specific theology of substitution and vicarious atonement. In Mesopotamian and Egyptian religion, animal sacrifice was common, but it typically functioned as a gift or propitiation, not as a substitute for human guilt. The Israelite practice of having the offerer (or their representative) lay hands on the animal and then having it killed created a visible, tangible connection between the human transgressor and the animal victim. This made clear that the death of the animal was not arbitrary punishment but a substitution for the death the transgressor deserved. The practice also served to create a moment of emotional and spiritual acknowledgment: the moment of hand-laying was the congregation's confrontation with the cost of their transgression, rendered visible through the animal's flesh. Requiring the elders to perform semikhah ensured that community leadership took visible responsibility for the congregation's instruction and welfare. If the congregation sinned through ignorance, it often reflected a failure of the elders to properly teach the law; by laying hands on the bull, the elders participated in their own atonement alongside the people's.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle of semikhah—laying hands to identify with and represent—appears throughout the Book of Mormon. In Mosiah 23:17, Alma ordains priests by laying on of hands. In D&C 42:38–39 (not technically BOM but Restoration context), the Lord establishes that ordination occurs 'by the laying on of the hands of the church.' The physical act of laying on of hands communicates identification, authority, and transferal of responsibility. In the BOM context, when Nephite leaders lay hands on others, they are not transferring guilt but blessing and authority. However, the principle of one person or group acting representatively for a larger community through physical gesture remains constant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:33 teaches that 'whoso is faithful unto the obtaining these two priesthoods...obtaineth all that his Father hath,' suggesting that priesthood functions as a representative and substitutionary office. The elders in Leviticus 4:15 similarly represent the congregation before God. D&C 76:53 describes the exaltation as entering into God's presence; the congregation's offering is a temporary provisional restoration of access to God's presence after transgression has ruptured it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the modern temple, the laying on of hands by priesthood officers is foundational to ordinances—blessings, sealing, ordinations. The principle is the same as semikhah: one person, acting representatively through priesthood authority, places hands on another to identify with them, bless them, or transfer authority. The congregation's elders in verse 15 are functioning in a priestly representative capacity, just as temple workers do in modern ordinances. The temple remains the place where substitutionary and representative atonement is both remembered and experienced through ordinance.

commentary.christological_typology: The laying on of hands on the sacrificial bull is the supreme type of Christ's substitutionary atonement. Just as the congregation's guilt is transferred to the bull through semikhah, all the sin of humanity is transferred to Christ through His covenant to become our substitute. Hebrews 10:5–10 describes Christ's entry into the world with the intention to do God's will: 'then said I, Lo, I come...to do thy will, O God.' This echoes the principle in verse 15: the innocent victim consents to bear the guilt. Isaiah 53:4–6 is the great Old Testament prophecy of this: 'Surely he hath borne our griefs...he was wounded for our transgressions...the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.' The laying on of hands in the Levitical chata't anticipates the laying on of sins upon the Messiah. Christ's death, like the bull's death, is vicarious—it effects what the congregation's death could not: true atonement and restoration of covenant relationship.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 15 teaches the principle that corporate communities are represented by leaders who bear responsibility before God. Members should recognize that when their leaders (bishops, stake presidents, General Authorities) stand before the Lord on behalf of the Church, they are exercising a representational function analogous to the elders laying hands on the bull. This creates two applications: First, members should sustain their leaders in this role, understanding that leaders bear accountability for the spiritual welfare of those they represent. Second, members should understand that through their leaders' priesthood, they themselves are bound in covenant before the Lord. The laying on of hands also teaches the principle of identification: true atonement requires that we identify ourselves with the substitute—in modern context, with Christ. This is not merely intellectual assent but a form of spiritual hand-laying, where we accept Christ's substitutionary work and allow ourselves to be identified with His perfect life and atoning death. In covenants made in temples and sacrament prayers, modern members renew this identification with Christ, just as the congregation identified with the bull through the elders' semikhah.

text_kjv: And the priest that is anointed shall bring of the bullock's blood to the tabernacle of the congregation:

commentary.narrative: Verse 16 introduces the anointed priest (kohen hamashiach) who will administer the congregation's purification. This is the same high priest who, in verses 3–12, offered a purification offering for his own sin. Now he stands in his official capacity to mediate the congregation's atonement. The fact that the same priest who addressed his own contamination now addresses the community's suggests a theology of priestly representation: the priest's role transcends his individual status; he is the Lord's agent of purification, whether the sin to be atoned is his own or the people's. He brings some of the bull's blood into the tabernacle (ohel mo'ed)—not to the outer altar (which will receive blood in verse 18) but into the sanctuary structure itself, the sacred inner space. This movement of blood deeper into the sanctuary mirrors the movement in verses 5–7, when the high priest took blood from his own offering into the Holy Place. The principle is consistent: blood penetration into the sanctuary's interior indicates the severity of contamination. Communal sin, like priestly sin, requires that blood reach inward to address the sanctuary's defilement at the deepest level.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb "bring" (hebi) emphasizes an active, purposeful movement. The priest does not casually carry the blood but deliberately bears it into God's presence. The blood is described as "of the bullock's blood" (min-dam hapar)—some portion of the total blood, not necessarily all of it. As verse 18 will show, the remaining blood is poured out at the base of the outer altar, but this portion, taken first, is directed inward toward the veil and the incense altar. The priest's action represents the congregation's entry point into atonement: their sacrifice has been slain, the blood has been shed (the life has been poured out), and now the medium of atonement—blood—is presented to the Lord in the sanctuary itself. This is the congregation's opportunity, represented by the priest, to stand before God with their sin-debt paid by substitute death and to receive the blessing of restored covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: The anointed priest; specifically the high priest or chief priest, who is set apart through anointing with sacred oil. Mashiach (anointed) becomes the title for the Messiah, the ultimate anointed one.
word_study.significance: The high priest is not merely one priest among many; he is the mashiach, the one consecrated through anointing to perform the most sacred functions. His unique anointing status is what qualifies him to enter the inner sanctuary and perform the blood ritual. The term meshiach anticipates the Messiah, emphasizing the redemptive, representative office of the anointed priest. In later rabbinical thought, this priest was understood as standing in an almost priestly-Messiah role—a type of the ultimate Redeemer.

word_study.meaning: To bring, to carry, or to cause to come. In sacrificial context, to present or deliver something to a sacred location or recipient.
word_study.significance: Hebi emphasizes the priest's active role in the purification process. He does not merely receive the blood; he brings it, transporting it purposefully into the sanctuary. This active transport of blood into the holy space is the priest's mediation of the congregation's atonement. Without the priest bringing the blood into the sanctuary, the congregation's substitutionary death would not effect purification.

word_study.meaning: Blood; the life-fluid of the animal, understood in Israelite theology as the seat of life (nefesh) and the medium of atonement.
word_study.significance: Blood is the central sacrificial element. Leviticus 17:11 explicitly states: 'For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls.' Blood is not merely a physical substance but carries theological weight as the substitute for life. The congregation's guilt has resulted in a death-debt; the bull's blood, representing its life poured out, effects atonement by satisfying that death-debt. The priest's handling and transport of blood is not a gruesome act but a sacred transaction.

word_study.meaning: The blood of the young bull; blood derived from the specific animal slaughtered as the congregation's sin offering.
word_study.significance: The blood is identified specifically as coming from the bull that was identified with the congregation through semikhah. This continuity is crucial: the same animal that the elders laid hands upon is the same animal whose blood effects the congregation's purification. There is no substitution of animals; the blood brought to the sanctuary comes from the precise bull that the congregation offered.

word_study.meaning: The tent of meeting; the portable sanctuary and the Lord's earthly dwelling place among His people.
word_study.significance: The tabernacle is the sacred space where atonement is mediated and God's presence dwells. By bringing blood into the ohel mo'ed, the priest is entering the sacred geography where purification is accomplished. The blood's entry into the sanctuary mirrors the congregation's spiritual reentry into covenant relationship with the Lord.

cross_references.connection: The high priest's own purification offering follows the identical procedure: the anointed priest brings blood into the tabernacle, establishing that communal sin requires the same depth of purification as priestly sin.

Christ, as the high priest of the new covenant, enters 'not made with hands' into the heavenly tabernacle 'by his own blood,' providing eternal purification; directly parallels the high priest bringing blood into the earthly tabernacle.

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest brings the blood of both the bullock and the goat within the veil to make atonement; the principle of priestly mediation of communal sin is extended to the annual purification of the entire nation.
Aaron must make atonement on the horns of the incense altar once a year with blood of the purification offering; establishes the ongoing need for priestly mediation in the sanctuary.
'The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin'; applies the Levitical principle that blood effects purification and atonement to Christ's redemptive work.

commentary.historical_context: In the tabernacle and later temple system, the high priest was the only person authorized to enter the inner sanctuary (the Holy Place and, once yearly, the Holy of Holies). This exclusive access reflected his special anointing and his role as the mediator between Israel and God. The anointing of the high priest with sacred oil (described in Exodus 29 and Leviticus 8) was a ceremony that set him apart and consecrated him for this mediatorial role. When the high priest brought blood into the tabernacle, he was exercising a function that no other Israelite—not the elders, not the congregation, not even ordinary priests—could perform. This created a hierarchical relationship: the congregation's guilt required the high priest's mediation; the people could not approach God directly to effect their own atonement. The requirement for priestly mediation reflects a theology of holiness as something that requires intermediary access. The blood itself, in ancient Israelite understanding, was not merely a physical substance but a sacred thing—the locus of life and atonement. Handling blood in the sanctuary required ritual purity and proper intention.
