The priest's transport of blood into the tabernacle was therefore a grave and solemn act, performed with awareness of its cosmic significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, King Benjamin and other prophets function as high priests who mediate the people's covenant relationship with God. In Mosiah 5, King Benjamin gathers the entire people and speaks to them concerning their covenant obligations and God's goodness, functioning as the anointed representative who brings the people into God's presence. The principle of priestly mediation—that the people need a sanctified representative to stand before the Lord on their behalf—is consistent throughout the BOM.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:33–34 teaches that those who obtain the priesthood and magnify their calling receive access to God's presence and understanding. D&C 76:50–60 describes those who become priests in the house of God, partakers of the priesthood of Aaron and the priesthood of Melchizedek. The principle is parallel: priestly authority, received through proper ordination and anointing, qualifies individuals to serve as mediators between God and the people. In modern restoration context, priesthood holders who perform ordinances are functioning in a manner analogous to the high priest bringing blood into the sanctuary—they are bringing the people's covenant offerings before the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The modern temple is the continuation of the tabernacle and temple system. Temple workers, authorized and 'anointed' through their calling, bring the people's prayers and covenants before the Lord through their performance of ordinances. Just as the high priest was the only authorized person to enter the Holy Place and Holy of Holies, temple workers (and specifically the president of the temple) have unique access to the most sacred spaces. The principle of priestly mediation remains: the congregation approaches God through authorized representatives, and the blood of Christ (symbolized in the sacrament and in temple ordinance language) effects their purification and atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: The anointed priest bringing blood into the tabernacle is the supreme type of Jesus Christ, the High Priest of the New Covenant, who brought His own blood into the heavenly sanctuary. Hebrews 9:11–12 states: 'But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.' Just as the earthly high priest brought the congregation's sacrificial blood into the tabernacle, Christ brought His own blood (His life poured out) into the heavenly sanctuary, effecting an eternal purification that the animal offerings could only foreshadow. Hebrews 10:19–20 invites believers to enter the holy place 'by the blood of Jesus...by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.' The veil that separated the congregation from direct access to God's presence in the tabernacle is torn aside through Christ's sacrifice. The congregation no longer depends on the high priest as intermediary; through Christ, all believers become priests with direct access to God.
commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints should recognize that authorized priesthood leaders continue the role of the anointed priest in bringing the congregation's covenants before the Lord. Just as the high priest was the indispensable mediator for communal atonement, modern leaders (bishops, stake presidents, temple presidents) serve as mediators in bringing the people's offerings and prayers before the Lord. Members should sustain their leaders in this role with faith that through proper priesthood authority, their individual and collective covenants are presented acceptably before God. Additionally, members should understand that through the atonement of Christ, all believers have become priests with access to the Father through Christ's blood. The ordinances of the temple renew this principle: through proper covenant-making and through the symbols and language of the temple, members participate in bringing their own offerings before the Lord, through Christ's atoning blood. This means living in a way that honors the sacrifice and maintains the sanctity of those covenants—essentially, keeping oneself clean and acceptable before the Lord through righteousness and repentance.

text_kjv: And the priest shall dip his finger in some of the blood, and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD, even before the vail.

commentary.narrative: Verse 17 describes the specific ritual act by which the high priest applies the blood within the Holy Place. The priest dips his finger into the blood—a gesture of intimate, precise handling—and sprinkles (nazah) the blood seven times before the Lord, specifically before the veil (parokhet) that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. This is an exact parallel to verse 6, which describes the identical procedure for the high priest's own sin offering. The fact that the congregation's purification follows the same blood procedure as the priest's individual purification underscores a radical theological equality: communal sin and individual priestly sin produce equivalent contamination in the sanctuary and require equivalent remediation. The seven sprinklings are symbolic of completeness and totality (seven being the sacred number in Israel); the sprinkling encompasses the totality of contamination and the totality of purification. Each sprinkling is an act of atonement, a presentation of the life-blood to the Lord before the veil where His presence particularly dwells.
commentary.narrative_continued: The veil (parokhet) is the curtain that hung within the tabernacle, separating the Holy Place (where the menorah, table of shewbread, and incense altar stood) from the Holy of Holies (where the ark of the covenant rested and where the Lord's presence was most intensely localized). The blood's application before the veil—not beyond it, but in its presence—represents the congregation's approach to God's holiness without transgressing the boundary of human access. The sprinkling is directed at the veil itself, as if the blood is being lifted up toward the Lord who dwells in the innermost chamber. This is a moment of intense spiritual transaction: the congregation's guilt, represented in the animal's blood, is presented directly to the source of holiness, asking for acceptance and forgiveness. The dipping of the finger (rather than, for example, pouring blood in a stream) conveys precision and control—the priest is not wildly flingling blood but carefully, ritually applying it in measured strokes. This precision reflects the solemnity of the moment and the priest's awareness that he is handling the instrument of atonement.

word_study.meaning: To dip, immerse, or soak. The finger is dipped into the blood, taking up a small amount on its tip.
word_study.significance: Tabal suggests a deliberate, controlled action: the finger is inserted into the blood and withdrawn, carrying a small portion on its tip. This is distinct from washing or flooding; it is a precise extraction of blood for ritual application. The method (dipping finger rather than using a vessel) emphasizes the intimacy and physicality of the ritual.

word_study.meaning: To sprinkle, to scatter, to throw drops, or to spatter. In sacrificial context, hazah denotes the ritualistic sprinkling of blood, which effects atonement.
word_study.significance: Hazah is the technical term for the ritual sprinkling of blood in the sanctuary. It is distinguished from mere pouring (yatzaq) of blood. Hazah conveys the idea of scattered drops, each drop carrying atonement, each sprinkling an act of petition before God. The Covenant Rendering appropriately uses 'sprinkle' to capture the sense of multiple discrete actions of application.

word_study.meaning: Seven times; seven repetitions of the action. Seven is the sacred, complete number in Israelite theology, associated with wholeness, sanctity, and fulfillment.
word_study.significance: The number seven is not arbitrary. In Levitical theology, seven represents completeness and the fullness of the sacred realm. Seven days of the week, seven years, seven times seven years (Jubilee)—seven is the marker of God's order and holiness. That the blood is sprinkled seven times indicates that the atonement is complete and total, addressing the sin in all its dimensions. The repetition seven times also creates a sense of intensity and emphasis: the congregation's need for atonement is grave enough to warrant the fullest ritual expression.

word_study.meaning: In the presence of, before, or in the sight of the Lord; in sacred space where God's presence is localized.
word_study.significance: The repeated phrase 'before the LORD' (appearing in verses 15, 16, and 17) emphasizes that the congregation's atonement is transparently presented to God. This is not a hidden or private matter; it is enacted in the sacred space where God's presence dwells. The congregation's guilt and their substitute's death are both brought into God's presence for His acknowledgment and acceptance.

word_study.meaning: The veil or curtain within the tabernacle that separated the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. Also figuratively, any barrier between the human and divine realms.
word_study.significance: The parokhet represents the boundary of human access to God's presence. In Levitical theology, only the high priest, once yearly, could pass beyond the veil into the Holy of Holies. The sprinkling of blood before the veil is an act directed at the holiness beyond the veil—it is an approach to God's innermost presence without transgressing the boundary. The veil is both barrier and threshold; the blood is sprinkled toward it, addressing the Lord who dwells within.

cross_references.connection: The identical procedure: the high priest dips his finger in blood and sprinkles it seven times before the LORD, before the veil, for his own sin offering; establishes the equivalence between priestly and communal purification.

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest sprinkles blood before the mercy seat (above the veil, in the Holy of Holies) seven times for the nation; the principle of seven-fold sprinkling for comprehensive atonement is central to Israel's annual purification.

'Without shedding of blood is no remission' (of sins); the sprinkling of blood in verse 17 enacts this principle—only through blood application can sin be atoned and the sanctuary's holiness be restored.
Christ is 'the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel'; applies the language of sprinkling and blood to Christ's atonement.

'Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ'; indicates that believers are sanctified through the sprinkling of Christ's blood, an application of Levitical atonement theology to the new covenant.

commentary.historical_context: The tabernacle's architecture placed the veil at a critical juncture: it marked the boundary beyond which ordinary Israelites could not pass. Only the high priest, and only on the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), could move beyond the veil into the Holy of Holies. This architectural restriction embodied a theology of holiness as increasingly intense as one approached God's presence. The Holy Court (open air) was accessible to all Israel. The Holy Place (inner sanctuary) was accessible only to priests in their officiating capacity. The Holy of Holies was accessible only to the high priest, once yearly. The sprinkling of blood before the veil (in the Holy Place, not beyond it) was therefore an act of extreme sanctity: the high priest stood before the ultimate boundary of his access, standing before the veil as the congregation's representative, presenting their atonement-blood to the Lord who dwelt beyond. The seven sprinklings, performed in measured repetition, created a moment of intense ritual and theological significance. This was not quick or mechanical; it was solemn, intentional, and laden with meaning. The congregation, watching from outside the sanctuary (or learning of the ritual through report), would understand that their representative priest was standing at the boundary of God's presence, presenting their blood-sacrifice and seeking the Lord's acceptance of their atonement.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 5:21–22, Alma asks his people if they feel to sing the songs of redeeming love, indicating that they have experienced a spiritual cleansing and atonement. The principle of sprinkling (nazah) as atonement parallels the anointing and blessing language used throughout the Book of Mormon when the Spirit sanctifies and purifies the people. Nephi's vision (1 Nephi 11) includes scenes of the Lamb of God coming down from heaven, which prefigures the ultimate offering whose blood will sprinkle and sanctify all who receive it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:3–5 describes Christ as the 'Only Begotten' who 'glorified' the Father by keeping all the commandments, and who stands 'in the midst' of the Father's presence, offering Himself as the 'great and last sacrifice.' This echoes the imagery of verse 17: Christ stands before the Father (before the veil, in a sense) offering His blood for the congregation of the righteous. D&C 76:50–60 describes those who obtain the priesthood and the promise of exaltation, having been 'sanctified by the Holy Ghost'; the sanctification parallels the purification through blood-sprinkling in verse 17.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the modern temple, the veil that separates the terrestrial room from the celestial room symbolizes the boundary between the human and divine realms, paralleling the parokhet in the tabernacle. Temple ordinances include ritual washings and anointings that symbolize purification and sanctification, analogous to the blood-sprinkling in verse 17. The movement through the temple, from entrance to the sanctum sanctorum (the celestial room), parallels the theological geography of the tabernacle, where movement inward requires increasing degrees of sanctity and proper authority. The veil ceremony in the temple represents the moment when authorized individuals approach the ultimate threshold before God.

commentary.christological_typology: The high priest's sprinkling of blood seven times before the veil is a type of Christ's entry into the heavenly sanctuary and His presentation of His blood before the Father. Hebrews 9:11–12 explicitly applies this imagery to Christ: 'But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands...by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.' The seven sprinklings, representing complete and perfect atonement, anticipate Christ's single, perfect offering that accomplishes all that the repeated animal sacrifices could only foreshadow. Hebrews 10:12 states: 'But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God.' The completeness of Christ's atonement—His ability to present His blood once and for all before the Father—is the fulfillment of the seven-fold sprinkling; it is the atonement that needs no repetition because it is exhaustively complete.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 17 teaches that atonement requires the presentation of blood (Christ's blood, through covenant participation) before God's holiness. When members partake of the sacrament, they are symbolically receiving the sprinkling of Christ's blood; they are participating, through ordinance, in the atonement that the high priest could only foreshadow. The emphasis on seven (completeness) should remind members that Christ's atonement is complete and sufficient; there is no sin beyond its reach, no transgression too great for it to remedy. Members should approach the veil (symbolically, in prayer and temple worship) with confidence that through Christ's blood-offering, they can stand before the Lord's holiness and be accepted. Furthermore, the precision and solemnity of the sprinkling should inspire members to approach their own repentance and covenant-keeping with similar seriousness. Just as the priest could not casually or carelessly perform the sprinkling, members cannot casually treat their covenants or their need for repentance. The sprinkling was an act of intense focus and intention; so should members' approach to their own purification and sanctification through Christ's atonement.

text_kjv: And he shall put some of the blood upon the horns of the altar which is before the LORD, that is in the tabernacle of the congregation, and shall pour out all the blood at the bottom of the altar of the burnt offering, which is at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18 completes the blood application procedure and mirrors verse 7 exactly, establishing the full parallel between the high priest's individual purification offering and the congregation's communal offering. The priest applies blood to the horns of the inner incense altar (the altar of sweet incense that stood before the Lord in the Holy Place, directly before the veil), and then pours the remaining blood at the base of the outer altar of burnt offering (the brazen altar that stood in the court at the tabernacle entrance). This dual application—inner altar horns and outer altar base—represents the full extent of the sanctuary's sacred geography and the totality of the purification. The blood reaches from the innermost point of the sanctuary (the area most immediately before God's presence, marked by the incense altar) down to the outermost point of the sacred precinct (the altar of burnt offering). This two-altar procedure indicates that the contamination caused by the congregation's sin penetrates the entire sanctuary—from the holiest place to the threshold—and therefore requires purification that spans the entire sacred space.
commentary.narrative_continued: The horns of the altar are protrusions that extended from the four corners of the altar's top surface. In ancient Israelite custom, the horns of the altar served as a place of refuge (1 Kings 1:50, 2:28); their symbolism connected them with power and divine protection. When blood was applied to the horns, it consecrated them and, by extension, sanctified the entire altar. The pouring out of the remaining blood at the base of the altar had both practical and theological functions: practically, it allowed the blood to drain away from the sacrificial site; theologically, it represented the life being entirely given over to the Lord, with nothing withheld. The base of the altar was the point where the sanctuary touched the ground, the boundary between the sacred precinct and the profane world. Blood poured at the base sealed the covenant transaction: the life is entirely surrendered to the Lord, and through this complete surrender, atonement is accomplished. Verse 18 presents a completed action: the blood application is finished, the congregation's purification ritual is concluded. The bull has been sacrificed, the blood has been brought into the sanctuary and applied at the two cardinal points of the sacred topography, and the atonement is effectuated. The congregation has been restored to covenant standing.

word_study.meaning: To put, to place, or to give. Natan emphasizes the action of setting something in a location, and in covenantal context, giving as an offering to the Lord.
word_study.significance: The priest places blood on the horns as a gift-offering to the Lord, an act of presentation and dedication. The verb carries the sense of deliberate placement, not casual action.

word_study.meaning: The four projections extending from the corners of an altar's top surface. In ancient Near Eastern architecture and symbolism, horns represented power, strength, and divine blessing.
word_study.significance: The horns of the altar were the most sacred part of the sacrificial installation; they were the points where blood was applied for purification and sanctification. In later Jewish tradition, the horns became symbols of the power of atonement. Grasping the horns of the altar became a gesture of seeking mercy and asylum. The blood applied to the horns sanctified them and consecrated the entire altar to the Lord's service.

word_study.term_english: altar which is before the LORD
word_study.meaning: The altar that stands before the LORD; the incense altar (altar of sweet incense) that stood in the Holy Place directly before the veil.
word_study.significance: This inner altar is distinguished from the outer altar of burnt offering (mentioned later in the verse). The incense altar was specifically located in the inner sanctuary, closest to the veil and God's presence. Blood application to this altar signifies purification at the deepest level of the sanctuary.

word_study.meaning: The tent of meeting; the portable sanctuary.
word_study.significance: Repeated here to clarify that the inner altar being referenced is located within the tabernacle (as opposed to the outer altar, which stands at the entrance to the tabernacle).

word_study.meaning: To pour, to spill, or to shed. In the context of blood, it denotes the complete outpouring and surrender of the life-substance.
word_study.significance: Shafakh emphasizes the totality of the blood's commitment to the Lord. All the remaining blood is poured out; nothing is retained. This represents complete submission and the entire surrender of the life-force to atone for the congregation's transgression.

word_study.meaning: Foundation, base, or the lowest part. In the context of the altar, the area at ground level where blood would drain or collect.
word_study.significance: The blood poured at the yesod (base/foundation) of the altar represents the life being given completely to God, with the blood returning to earth as the life-substance. The base is the point of contact between the sacred altar and the profane world, suggesting that the blood purifies the boundary between sacred and secular space.

word_study.meaning: The altar of burnt offering; the outer altar in the tabernacle court, where animals were slaughtered and burnt offerings were made.
word_study.significance: This altar is distinguished from the inner incense altar. It is the place where the sacrificial animal is killed and where public offerings are made. Blood application to this outer altar completes the purification process that began at the inner altar.

word_study.meaning: Door, entrance, or opening; the threshold or boundary of a sacred space.
word_study.significance: The altar of burnt offering stood at the entrance (petach) to the tabernacle, marking the boundary where the sacred precinct begins. Blood poured at this boundary altar seals the atonement at the outermost point of the sanctuary.

cross_references.connection: Identical procedure for the high priest's personal sin offering: blood is put on the horns of the inner altar and poured out at the base of the outer altar; establishes the equivalence between priestly and communal purification.

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest applies blood to the horns of the outer altar to 'make an atonement for the holy place' and 'for the altar'; the two-altar application is central to Israel's comprehensive national purification.

Instructions for the consecration of Aaron: blood of the sacrificial bull is put on the horns of the altar and poured out at the base; establishes the two-altar procedure as foundational to Levitical sacrifice.
Adonijah 'caught hold of the horns of the altar' seeking sanctuary; illustrates that the horns of the altar were understood as a place of power and refuge, a symbol of God's protection.

'We have an altar, whereof they have no right to eat which serve the tabernacle...Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate'; applies the outer altar imagery to Christ's death outside the city, and the sanctifying power of His blood to all believers.

commentary.historical_context: The two-altar system in the tabernacle and later temple represented a vertical and horizontal axis of the sacred cosmos in Israelite theology. The incense altar stood in the Holy Place before the veil, representing the approach to God's immediate presence; the burnt offering altar stood in the outer court, representing the public, communal dimension of sacrifice. Blood application to both altars signified that purification extended throughout the sanctuary's entire sacred geography. In the tabernacle arrangement, the inner altar of incense stood about 10 cubits from the veil, directly opposite the entrance to the Holy Place. The outer altar of burnt offering stood some 40 cubits distant, in the court. The blood's journey from inner altar to outer altar—from the holiest place to the threshold of the sanctuary—symbolically addressed the full extent of contamination. The pouring of blood at the base of the outer altar also had practical significance: it prevented the blood from being trampled or allowed to run into the secular world; instead, it was contained at the boundary of the sacred precinct. This practice reflected the principle that sacred substances must be handled with care and must not be profaned by common use. The horns of the altar, being prominent and conspicuous, also served a visibility function: the blood visible on the horns announced to all who approached the sanctuary that atonement had been made and that the altar had been consecrated for its redemptive function.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon does not contain explicit parallels to the two-altar blood application procedure, but the principle of comprehensive sanctification appears throughout. In 1 Nephi 11:24–33, Nephi's vision includes the descent of the Lamb of God and the sprinkling of His blood, which serves to sanctify and purify all things. The symbolism in verse 18—blood reaching from the innermost to the outermost, from the most sacred to the threshold—suggests a comprehensive redemption that extends to all people, regardless of where they stand in relation to God's presence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:50–60 describes those who become 'thrones, principalities, and powers, or dominions,' having been 'sanctified by the Holy Ghost'; the comprehensive sanctification suggested by verse 18's two-altar application is fulfilled in the sanctification of all who receive Christ's atonement. D&C 138:16–19 describes the Savior's visit to the spirits in the spirit world, 'declaring liberty to the captives who were bound...declaring the acceptable day of the Lord'; the blood application that frees and cleanses the congregation from sin (verse 18) is a foreshadowing of Christ's universal redemptive work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The modern temple contains layers of sacred space corresponding to the tabernacle's two-altar system: the baptismal font (representing purification at the threshold), the various ordinance rooms (representing movement through sacred space), and ultimately the celestial room (representing the Holy of Holies). The progression from outer to inner, from threshold to the most sacred chamber, mirrors the two-altar procedure. Temple covenants, made at various points within the temple, represent the comprehensive commitment of the individual to God—from the initial covenant of baptism through the final sealing covenant, much as the congregation's blood covers the entire sanctuary from inner altar to outer.

commentary.christological_typology: The pouring of blood at the base of the altar, representing the complete outpouring of the congregation's life-substitute, is the supreme type of Christ's complete self-offering. Isaiah 53:12 prophesies that the Servant 'poured out his soul unto death'; John 19:34 records that when a soldier pierced Christ's side, 'forthwith came there out blood and water.' The totality of the blood application—reaching from the innermost sanctuary to the outermost boundary—foreshadows the universal scope of Christ's atonement: 'That Christ by the grace of God should taste death for every man' (Hebrews 2:9). The two-altar application symbolizes the reach of the atonement: inward to the deepest recesses of the human soul (represented by the inner altar) and outward to all humanity (represented by the outer altar and the base where all can witness it). Hebrews 9:13–14 makes the comparison explicit: 'For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?' The Levitical blood application at two altars is rendered perfect and eternal in Christ's single, all-encompassing offering.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 18 teaches that Christ's atonement is comprehensive and complete, reaching to all who will receive it—from the most righteous to the most afflicted, from those at the center of the Church to those on the periphery. Just as the congregation's blood covered the entire sanctuary, Christ's blood covers all aspects of human need: spiritual contamination (sin), physical ailment (healing), emotional wounds (comfort), and relational rupture (reconciliation). Members should approach Christ's atonement with confidence that it is sufficient for their particular circumstances. Furthermore, the dual application of blood suggests that atonement operates at multiple levels: at the inner, personal level of conscience and heart (inner altar), and at the outer, communal level of society and relationships (outer altar). This means repentance and atonement should extend to both personal reformation and relational reconciliation; members should seek to be cleansed not only before God but also within their relationships and communities. Finally, the completeness of the procedure—nothing withheld, all blood poured out—should inspire members to wholehearted commitment to covenant. Just as the priest poured out all remaining blood (not holding some back), members should give their whole heart, might, mind, and strength to keeping their covenants. Partial commitment, like partial blood application, would not effect complete atonement.

text_kjv: And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat is taken away from off the sacrifice of peace offerings; and the priest shall burn it upon the altar for a sweet savour unto the LORD; and the priest shall make an atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him.

commentary.narrative: Verse 31 concludes the sin offering procedure for the common person (introduced in v27). The offerer brings a female goat, lays hands upon it, slaughters it at the altar of burnt offering, and now the priest removes the fat in the exact same manner as the fat from a peace offering is removed. This deliberate comparison to the peace offering is significant: the peace offering celebrates communion with God, yet here the sin offering uses the same fat-handling procedure. The fat—the richest part of the animal, already reserved for God in other sacrifices—is now turned into smoke as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The language 'pleasing aroma' (reiach niychoach) appears throughout Leviticus whenever God accepts a sacrifice, signaling divine approval and completion of the ritual.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse concludes with the definitive priestly declaration: 'the priest shall make an atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him.' This is the fourth and final time in Leviticus 4 that this exact formula (kipper... veniselach lo) appears—in verses 20 (high priest), 26 (congregation), 31 (commoner), and again in verse 35 (commoner with lamb). The translator notes reveal the profound theological symmetry: the high priest receives the same complete forgiveness as the poorest commoner. The graduated procedures (bull versus goat, inner versus outer altar) do not produce graduated forgiveness. This verse demonstrates that the chata't (sin offering) system was designed with pastoral genius: every Israelite, regardless of status or wealth, has access to the same complete atonement. The variation in offerings reflects economic reality, not theological value.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The Covenant Rendering's translation of the opening phrase—'All its fat he shall remove'—captures a nuance important for understanding: this is not optional removal but a prescribed action. The priest's handling of the fat is part of the ritual's holiness; improper treatment would render the offering defective. The comparison to the shelamim (peace offering) appears for the fourth time in this chapter (vv. 10, 19 implied, 26, 31), creating a literary and theological anchor: just as peace offerings maintain the relationship between Israel and God through communion, the sin offering maintains the sanctuary's purity, which undergirds that relationship. Without atonement for sin, the sanctuary becomes defiled and communion is impossible.
commentary.narrative_continued_3: From a modern reader's perspective, this verse may seem repetitive—why include such detailed instructions about fat removal when the same procedure appears in verses 10, 26, and will appear again in 35? The answer lies in the ancient world's understanding of ritual. Repetition was not seen as redundancy but as authority and solemnity. Each repetition reinforced the non-negotiability of the procedure and the equality of access. An Israelite bringing a goat to the altar would see themselves performing the identical procedure as the high priest with a bull—a powerful statement of covenantal equality in the face of God.

cross_references.connection: Identical conclusion formula (kipper... veniselach lo) for the congregation's sin offering, showing that atonement and forgiveness are identical regardless of who brings the offering.
The peace offering (shelamim) procedure that Lev 4:31 explicitly references for fat removal, demonstrating how sin offerings borrow the sanctification procedures of communion offerings.
The burnt offering also produces a 'sweet savour unto the LORD,' linking the sin offering's acceptance to other accepted sacrifices and suggesting all properly performed sacrifices please God.
God speaks of blotting out transgressions and not remembering sins—the spiritual reality that the Levitical sin offering ritual makes possible and represents in physical form.
New Testament reflection that animal blood cannot take away sins, pointing to the ultimate and eternal nature of Christ's atonement compared to the repeated chata't offerings.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:25-35 discusses the justice and mercy balanced in the atonement plan—how the law demands payment for sin but divine mercy provides a way of escape. The Levitical sin offering embodies this principle: the law requires atonement (the ritual), but divine grace provides the means (the prescribed sacrifice). Similarly, Mosiah 15:7-9 emphasizes that Christ would 'suffer death, even the death of the cross...that he might bring salvation unto his people.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 110:11-13 records Joseph Smith's vision of the Kirtland Temple and references the 'sacrifice of a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' While D&C text does not explicitly reinterpret Levitical sacrifice, this principle suggests that inward contrition (the offerer's genuine repentance in bringing the offering) is the spiritual reality that the outward ritual manifests. The sin offering cannot work without sincerity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The structure of Leviticus 4 (blood on inner altar horns for priest and congregation; blood on outer altar horns for leader and commoner) mirrors temple theology about different levels of access and atonement. The high priest alone enters the inner sanctuary on Yom Kippur to atone for the whole nation. Yet even the commoner's offering—performed outside the inner sanctuary—accomplishes full atonement when performed according to covenant law. This parallels Latter-day Saint temple practice, where different ordinances serve different functions but all lead toward exaltation and the restoration of broken covenants.

commentary.historical_context: The commoner bringing a female goat represents the ordinary Israelite—the shepherd, the farmer, the merchant. The deliberate provision of a second, even more economical option (the female lamb in v. 32) reveals the system's pastoral design. In ancient economies, wealth was largely measured in animals; a female lamb represented the minimum sacrificial expense. Archaeological evidence from ancient Near Eastern temples shows that access to ritual purification was often restricted to the wealthy or high-ranking. Israel's sin offering system was radically different: it explicitly created a graduated schedule to ensure the poorest Israelite had a path to atonement. The removal of fat in the exact manner of peace offerings also reflects ancient Near Eastern understanding that the deity received the 'best part' of offerings (the fat, the organs) while people received the meat. This division appears across Mesopotamian and Egyptian temple practice, but Israel's innovation was universalizing access to both kinds of sacrifice—peace offerings for communion and sin offerings for restoration.

word_study.meaning: the fatty tissue, especially the internal fat surrounding the organs; in sacrificial contexts, the richest, most choice portion reserved exclusively for God's altar
word_study.significance: Cheleb appears throughout Leviticus as the portion that 'belongs to the LORD.' It was never to be eaten by common people (Lev 3:17; 7:23), making it the most sacred edible part of the animal. Its burning as a pleasing aroma symbolizes the most precious offering returning to God. The repeated comparison to shelamim (peace offering) fat removal suggests the sin offering shares the sacrificial dignity of communion offerings, not merely the practicality of disposal.

word_study.meaning: to cover, to atone, to wipe clean; in Levitical context, to restore sanctity to the sanctuary and remove the barrier sin creates between the offerer and God
word_study.significance: Kipper is the core verb of Leviticus 4. It is not mere forgiveness (which comes after) but active ritual restoration. The priest performs kipper; God grants the forgiveness (selach). This distinction matters: the human ritual enables divine forgiveness. The repeated use of kipper in v. 31 with the identical conclusion of forgiveness in every subsection of chapter 4 is theologically revolutionary—access to atonement is not limited by status but guaranteed by obedience to the prescribed ritual.

word_study.meaning: to be forgiven, to have sin remitted; passive voice indicating God's action, not the human's or the priest's
word_study.significance: This is consistently God's action, not the priest's accomplishment. The priest makes atonement (kipper); God grants forgiveness (selach). The structure of v. 31 mirrors vv. 20, 26, and 35: human action (removal of fat, burning, priestly declaration) enables divine response (forgiveness). This preserves both the necessity of human obedience to the ritual law and God's sovereignty in granting forgiveness.

word_study.meaning: literally 'a scent of rest' or 'aroma of soothing'; the smell of the burning sacrifice that signals God's acceptance and delight
word_study.significance: This phrase appears throughout the Pentateuch for accepted sacrifices (e.g., Genesis 8:21 after the flood). It indicates divine pleasure, not merely the acceptance of a transaction. Even a sin offering—brought to address transgression—produces a sweet aroma to God when performed properly. This suggests God finds pleasure not in punishing sin but in its remediation through the covenant's prescribed means.

commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Leviticus 4:31 teaches a crucial principle about repentance: atonement is not a luxury reserved for the spiritually elite but a covenant right available to every member who approaches through the prescribed means. Just as the commoner brought a female goat—not the most expensive or prestigious offering—modern members need not wait until they achieve perfect understanding or unwavering spirituality to seek repentance and forgiveness through Jesus Christ. The atonement is structured with your economic and spiritual reality in mind. The repetition of the forgiveness formula (kipper... veniselach lo) four times in Leviticus 4 should anchor modern testimony: God's forgiveness is not earned by the quality of your offering but granted when you follow the covenant path—confession, repentance, restitution where possible, and recommitment to covenant law. The 'sweet savour' that rises from honest repentance pleases God not because your effort is perfect but because your heart is turned toward Him.
commentary.christological_typology: Leviticus 4:31 prefigures Christ as the ultimate sin offering. The repeated emphasis that 'the priest shall make an atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him' points forward to Christ, who serves as both High Priest and sacrifice. Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts the repetitive nature of the Levitical sin offering—performed 'day by day' and 'often'—with Christ's single, eternal offering. The 'sweet savour' produced by the burnt fat of the animal sin offering finds its ultimate reality in the 'fragrant offering and sacrifice to God' of Christ (Ephesians 5:2). The commoner's access to atonement through the female goat or lamb speaks to Christ's availability to all—not restricted by status, wealth, or power. All who approach God through Christ find the same complete forgiveness.

text_kjv: And if he bring a lamb for a sin offering, he shall bring it a female without blemish.

commentary.narrative: Verse 32 introduces the second option available to the commoner: instead of a female goat (v. 28), the offerer may bring a female lamb as a sin offering. The specification 'female without blemish' (neqevah temimah) is absolute—not merely preferred but required. The word 'temimah' (complete, whole, perfect) demands that the animal have no defect visible to the examiner. In an agrarian economy where animals were a primary form of wealth, this requirement was significant: the offerer must surrender not merely an animal, but an unblemished one, suitable for breeding or market.
commentary.narrative_continued: The presentation of two options—goat (v. 28) and lamb (v. 32)—is the Levitical system's provision for economic reality. The translator notes are explicit: 'Two choices—goat (v28) or lamb (v32)—provide economic flexibility.' A female lamb was likely the least expensive sacrificial animal available. Modern readers often overlook how revolutionary this was in the ancient world. Temple systems in Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Canaan typically required specific animals regardless of the offerer's means. A poor farmer who could not afford a bull or even a goat might be excluded from ritual atonement. Israel's system created a graduated scale that ensured the poorest Israelite had a path to forgiveness. The inclusion of 'female' in both options (vv. 28, 32) may reflect the economic logic that a female animal, valuable for breeding, was still accessible to someone of limited means.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The emphasis on 'without blemish' (temimah) might seem to contradict the idea of accessibility—if the animal must be perfect, doesn't this burden the poor? However, in the ancient world, most domestic animals were unblemished; a blemished animal would be less valuable for work, breeding, or trade. The requirement of an unblemished animal was not a hidden barrier but a statement of covenant dignity: even the poorest Israelite's offering to God must be whole and complete. This reflects theological principle, not economic discrimination. The animal's perfection mirrors what God requires from the offerer—a 'broken and contrite heart' (Psalm 51:17), undivided commitment, wholeness of intention.

cross_references.connection: The parallel verse offering the goat as the first commoner option, establishing that the choice between goat (v. 28) and lamb (v. 32) both fulfill the sin offering requirement.

Leviticus 5 expands the sin offering with explicit graduated options for poor persons: a lamb, or two turtledoves, or a handful of fine flour, demonstrating the system's commitment to universal access.
The burnt offering likewise permits both male and female lambs, showing that the requirement for unblemished animals and the specification of sex applied across multiple offering types.
References Christ as 'a lamb without blemish and without spot'—the ultimate antitype of the unblemished lamb brought by the Levitical commoner, pointing to Christ's perfect atonement.

Though the Psalmist declares God does not delight in sacrifice itself, the broken and contrite heart is the internal reality the unblemished lamb externally represents—sincere repentance, not mere ritual compliance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 42:13-15 expounds on the law of restoration and mercy: justice demands that sin be punished, but mercy provides a way through obedience to law. The provision of the female lamb as an option for the commoner mirrors this doctrine—the law of sacrifice cannot be waived, but it is structured so that mercy is accessible to all who obey it, regardless of wealth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:34-39 speaks of the light by which all things are judged and the law that governs all things. The Levitical law's graduated structure reflects this principle—the law is immutable, yet it is merciful in its administration. The female lamb requirement shows that God's law accounts for human limitation while maintaining its standard.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The unblemished lamb brings to mind the temple recommend system in modern Latter-day Saint practice. Just as every person, regardless of wealth or status, may hold a temple recommend if they meet the same standards, every Israelite, regardless of economic station, could bring an unblemished animal and receive the same atonement. The 'female' specification may also resonate with temple covenants that emphasize the divine feminine—women's equal access to covenant and atonement.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, animal sacrifice was common to virtually all cultures, but the structure and accessibility of sacrifice varied significantly. Mesopotamian temples required specific animals depending on the type of offering and the offerer's status. Egyptian temples had elaborate hierarchies of sacrifice. The Hittite kingdom had detailed ritual prescriptions. Yet the Levitical system stands out for its explicit commitment to graduated affordability while maintaining theological uniformity of outcome. A female lamb, the smallest common domesticated animal in ancient Levant, was within reach of even subsistence-level families. Archaeological evidence from the Levantine regions shows that sheep herding was widespread even among the poorest communities. The specification of 'female without blemish' also reflects practical knowledge: a female animal had breeding value, making unblemished females economically significant property. By permitting either a goat or a lamb, the system accommodated both sheep-herding and goat-herding cultures within Israel, reflecting the diversity of the twelve tribes.

word_study.meaning: a young female sheep, typically in its first or second year; the smallest and most economically accessible sacrificial animal in the Levitical system
word_study.significance: Kevsah appears in contexts of both regular offerings and special circumstances. Its use as an option for the commoner's sin offering marks a critical theological statement: the smallest, most accessible animal can accomplish the same atonement as a bull. The lamb's humility and gentleness made it a symbolic fit for an offering addressing transgression and weakness.

word_study.meaning: whole, complete, unblemished, without defect; from the root tamam, meaning to be complete or finished
word_study.significance: Temimah is not merely aesthetic perfection but covenant completeness. The animal must be physically whole because it represents the offerer's desire to be spiritually whole. The Covenant Rendering preserves this nuance by rendering it 'unblemished.' An animal with a blemish—a missing eye, a broken horn, a limp—was considered incomplete and therefore unfit for sacrifice. This standard applied equally to the poorest commoner's lamb and the priest's bull, emphasizing that God's standard for holiness does not vary by economic status.

word_study.meaning: female; the grammatical and biological designation of a female animal
word_study.significance: The specification of female for both goat and lamb options (vv. 28, 32) is economically and theologically deliberate. A female animal retained reproductive value, making it potentially less expensive than a male, yet it was still a meaningful sacrifice. The Levitical system's attention to which sex of animal was appropriate for which offering reveals sophisticated economic thinking within theological language.

commentary.application: Leviticus 4:32 teaches modern covenant members that repentance is not a luxury for the spiritually advanced but an accessible pathway designed for ordinary people in ordinary circumstances. The female lamb represents the 'least' you can bring—your simplest acknowledgment of sin, your most basic commitment to change. The covenant does not require you to have achieved perfect understanding, perfect circumstances, or perfect spiritual maturity before you qualify for atonement. It requires honesty: the willingness to bring whatever you have, unblemished in its sincerity, and lay it before God through the priesthood. The repetition of two options (goat or lamb) should comfort modern members: God understands that your path, your resources, and your situation are unique. The atonement of Christ is structured to meet you where you are. What matters is that what you bring is whole-hearted, sincere, and submitted to the covenant process. That unblemished lamb—your honest, complete repentance—is all God requires.
commentary.christological_typology: The unblemished female lamb of Leviticus 4:32 is directly echoed in 1 Peter 1:19, where Christ is identified as 'a lamb without blemish and without spot.' The progression is striking: the commoner's female lamb—the smallest, most accessible offering—points to the ultimate Lamb whose sacrifice is perfect, permanent, and universally efficacious. The female specification may also reflect Christ's role in bearing the burden of human weakness. Isaiah 53:7 describes the Suffering Servant as 'brought as a lamb to the slaughter...yet he opened not his mouth.' The meek, submissive quality of the lamb as a sacrificial animal resonates with Christ's voluntary self-offering and patient acceptance of his mission.

text_kjv: And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering, and slay it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.

commentary.narrative: Verse 33 prescribes the procedural steps for the commoner's lamb sin offering, and these steps are identical to the procedure for the commoner's goat offering described in verse 29. The offerer 'shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering' (semikhah)—the formal action of identification and transfer of liability. By this action, the offerer identifies the animal as their representative, transferring their sin to it symbolically. The laying on of hands is the same ritual gesture used across multiple Levitical offerings, but in the sin offering context it carries particular weight: the animal is being designated to bear the offerer's transgression.
commentary.narrative_continued: The offerer then 'slays it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.' This location—the outer altar where burnt offerings are slaughtered—is significant. The commoner's sin offering is not performed in the inner sanctum (the inner altar where the priest's and congregation's sin offerings are performed) but at the outer, public altar. This distinction reflects both the severity of the sin (inner altar offenses are more grave) and the accessibility of atonement (the outer altar is accessible to all Israelites). The translator notes emphasize that 'the repetition across both commoner options (goat v28-31, lamb v32-35) ensures clarity: regardless of which animal the commoner chooses, the ritual is identical.' This repetition is pedagogically crucial. An Israelite reading or hearing these laws would understand that their choice between goat and lamb is purely economic; the spiritual outcome and the ritual procedure are unchanged.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The phrase 'slay it for a sin offering' (yishchat otah lechattah) uses the same verb (shachat, to slaughter) as ordinary meat butchering, yet here it is an act of covenant significance. The place of slaughter—at the outer altar—grounds the sin offering in public, communal space rather than private action. This prevents sin offering from becoming a secret, private transaction between an individual and God. Instead, it is a public, witnessed action performed in the sanctuary's most accessible location. The priest's role is to receive the animal, perform the slaughter in the specified location, and then handle the blood and fat according to the law (vv. 34-35). The offerer's role is to bring the unblemished animal, lay hands upon it, and observe the ritual's completion.

cross_references.connection: The parallel procedure for the commoner's goat sin offering, using identical language about laying hands and slaughtering at the outer altar, confirming that procedure is constant regardless of which animal is chosen.
The burnt offering procedure also requires laying hands on the animal's head, establishing semikhah as a consistent gesture of identification across multiple offering types.

The theological principle that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' and blood 'makes an atonement for your souls,' explaining why slaughter and blood-shedding are theologically necessary, not merely practical.
The Suffering Servant 'is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth'—the ultimate fulfillment of the animal's role as willing victim.
New Testament declaration that 'without shedding of blood is no remission of sins,' connecting the Levitical requirement of slaughter to the theological necessity of Christ's blood atonement.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 22:14 describes the shedding of blood as necessary for remission of sins, resonating with Leviticus 17:11. The Book of Mormon affirms the Levitical principle that sacrifice (and particularly blood-shedding) is covenant-requisite. Mosiah 13:27-32 explicitly states that the law of Moses 'was a type of that sacrifice which should come' in Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 20:77-79 describes the sacrament as a covenant renewal in which bread and water represent Christ's body and blood. The priest's blessing of the sacrament parallels the priest's reception and handling of the sacrifice in Levitical law. Both are acts of covenant mediation where the priesthood formally presents the offering (actual in Leviticus, symbolic in the sacrament) to God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The outer altar setting and the public nature of the commoner's sin offering find parallel in modern temple practice, where covenants made in the temple are personal but made in the presence of witnesses and administered through ordained priesthood holders. The location 'where they kill the burnt offering'—a place known to all Israel—suggests that sin offering, though personally applicable, is not hidden from the community. Modern covenant members, like ancient Israelites, make covenants through prescribed channels, in designated places, administered by authorized servants.

commentary.historical_context: The specification that sin offerings be slaughtered 'in the place where they kill the burnt offering' reflects the organized structure of the Israelite sanctuary. Archaeological understanding of tabernacle and temple layouts shows that the outer courtyard contained the bronze altar (the altar of burnt offering), where public sacrifices were performed in view of the assembled Israelites. This contrasts with inner altar procedures (on the golden altar of incense), which only the high priest could approach and which were hidden from public view. The distinction between outer and inner altar procedures served multiple functions: it maintained the sanctity of the inner sanctuary, it ensured the priesthood's mediatory role, and it accommodated different levels of sin severity. A commoner's unintentional sin was addressed at the outer, public altar; the high priest's sin (which threatened the entire nation) was addressed at the inner altar with elaborate procedures. This architectural and procedural distinction reveals sophisticated theological thinking about sin's varying impact on the covenant community.

word_study.meaning: to lay, press, or place one's hand upon; in sacrificial context, the act of identification and transference of sin from offerer to animal
word_study.significance: Semikhah (the noun form) appears in the Levitical sacrificial system as the formal gesture of identification. By laying hands on the animal's head, the offerer witnesses their own liability being transferred to the substitute. This is not merely ceremonial but theologically profound: the animal becomes the offerer's representative before God. The Hebrew verb samakh implies both physical contact and legal/relational transference. Leviticus 1:4 uses the identical term for burnt offerings, but in sin offerings the transference of sin (rather than dedication) is the focus.

word_study.meaning: to slaughter, kill, cut the throat; the practical method of animal sacrifice that ends the animal's life and enables blood to be collected for ritual use
word_study.significance: Shachat is the verb used across all Levitical sacrifices. The shedding of blood (through slaughter) is theologically necessary because, as Leviticus 17:11 states, 'the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement by reason of the life.' Slaughter is not incidental detail but core theology. The animal's death is not punishment inflicted on an innocent creature but a covenant act that makes atonement possible.

word_study.term_english: in the place where they kill the burnt offering
word_study.term_original: בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁחַט אֶת־הָעֹלָה (bimkom asher yischochat et-ha'olah)
word_study.meaning: at the location designated for burnt offering slaughter; the outer altar in the sanctuary courtyard, accessible to all Israelites
word_study.significance: The specification of location is theologically loaded. Inner altar procedures (used for priest and congregation) are performed in the inner sanctuary, closed to common Israelites. Outer altar procedures (used for leader and commoner) are public. By mandating that the commoner's sin offering be slaughtered at the outer altar—the same place as burnt offerings—the law signals that sin offering is not a shameful, hidden act but a normal, public covenant procedure. The outer altar is where ordinary Israelites habitually observe sacrificial activity.

commentary.application: Leviticus 4:33 teaches modern covenant members that genuine repentance requires personal identification with the atonement's cost. The laying on of hands signals that you are not merely observing someone else's sacrifice but actively participating in your own restoration. The slaughter—the death of the substitute—is not something to be hidden from or squeamish about but to witness with clear eyes, understanding that your sin has a real cost and that the covenant provides a real remedy. The location at the outer altar, in the presence of the community, teaches that repentance is not a private shame to be hidden but a normal, public act of covenant obedience. In modern practice, this translates to meeting with priesthood leaders, openly acknowledging sin through confession, and working through the prescribed steps of repentance within the community of faith. The specificity of Levitical procedure—exactly which animal, exactly where, exactly how—teaches that repentance is not vague feeling but concrete action through established channels. Your honest, humble participation in the covenant's redemptive process, witnessed and administered through priesthood authority, makes atonement operative in your life.
commentary.christological_typology: The commoner laying hands on the lamb and witnessing its slaughter prefigures the sinner's identification with Christ, whose blood is shed for remission of sins. The lamb's submission to slaughter—particularly as understood through Isaiah 53:7 ('as a lamb to the slaughter')—points to Christ's voluntary acceptance of his sacrificial role. The specification that slaughter occur 'in the place where they kill the burnt offering' also resonates with Golgotha's location outside the city walls—a public place where the ultimate Lamb was offered in full view of witnesses. The commoner's sin offering was not hidden or shameful but public and normal; similarly, Christ's crucifixion was public, witnessed, and the normal means by which God accomplishes redemption.

text_kjv: And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, and put it upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar:

commentary.narrative: Verse 34 describes the priest's blood manipulation for the commoner's sin offering—the final iteration of this procedure in Leviticus 4. The priest takes blood 'with his finger' (beetzba'o) and applies it to 'the horns of the altar of burnt offering' (qarnot mizbach ha'olah), then pours the remainder 'at the bottom of the altar' (el yesod hamizbach). This exact procedure is identical to verse 30 (the leader's sin offering) and parallel to verses 7 and 18 (priest and congregation, with the difference that their blood goes to the inner altar's horns). The translator notes highlight the structural significance: 'The final iteration of the blood-application procedure in the chapter. Across all four categories, the blood goes to only two possible destinations: the inner sanctuary (priest and congregation) or the outer altar (leader and commoner). This binary distinction is the structural backbone of the chata't system.'
commentary.narrative_continued: The application of blood 'with his finger' is deliberate: not with a cup or vessel, but with the priest's own body. This creates intimate, personal contact between priest, blood, and altar—the priest's agency and touch make the atonement operative. The 'horns of the altar' (qarnot hamizbach) were projections at the four corners of the altar, each one representing one direction. By marking all four corners with blood, the priest ensures the entire altar—and therefore the entire camp—is covered by the atoning blood. The horns were sacred: in legal contexts, a person fleeing for mercy could grasp the altar's horns (1 Kings 1:50-51; 2:28), making them symbols of both judgment and refuge.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The pouring of 'all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar' (et kol-dama yishpok el yesod hamizbach) ensures that the blood, which represents the life of the animal and the atonement's efficacy, returns completely to God. No blood is wasted or diverted; all of it serves the sanctification of the altar. This completeness mirrors the pattern throughout Leviticus 4: whether the animal is a bull, a goat, or a lamb—whether it belongs to priest, congregation, leader, or commoner—the blood accomplishes the same atonement when properly applied. The distinction between inner and outer altar (v. 34 uses the outer altar's horns and base, while vv. 7, 18 use the inner altar) reflects the gravity of the sin, but the blood's application is equally thorough in all cases.

cross_references.connection: Identical procedure for the leader's sin offering: blood applied to outer altar's horns and base, confirming that commoner and leader receive the same blood ritual despite their different animals and social status.

The priest's sin offering uses the inner altar's horns, showing the structural distinction between inner (for grave sins) and outer (for lesser sins) altar procedures while maintaining the same principle of horns and base blood application.

The theological foundation: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement by reason of the life.'
Without shedding of blood there is no remission of sins—the New Testament application of the Levitical principle that atonement requires blood's shedding and application.
The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin—the spiritual fulfillment of the cleansing efficacy symbolized in the priest's application of animal blood to the altar.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:10-14 teaches that Christ's blood 'shall be shed for the remission of sins' and that through his atonement 'all those who have faith in his redemption are saved.' The blood application in verse 34 is the shadow; Christ's blood shed once for all is the substance. The repeated, meticulous application of animal blood in the Levitical system points to the singular, perfect efficacy of Christ's blood.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:2 references the sacrament as a memorial of Christ's blood. Just as the priest in Leviticus 4:34 applies blood to the altar as the covenant's most sacred act, modern priesthood holders administer the sacrament as a covenant renewal, blessing water (in modern practice) or wine (symbolizing blood) as a memorial of Christ's atonement. The precision and formality of the sacramental blessing mirrors the precision of blood application in Levitical sacrifice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The application of blood—marking the altar's horns and base—parallels temple covenants, where certain tokens and signs are administered and certain locations within the temple are marked as especially sacred. The outer altar blood application, being accessible and observable by all Israelites (unlike inner sanctuary procedures), resonates with the role of temple endowment in making covenants accessible to all worthy members, not merely the ecclesiastical elite.

commentary.historical_context: The architectural detail that the outer altar (the bronze altar in the courtyard) had horns is archaeologically and textually confirmed. Ancient Near Eastern altars characteristically had horns—projections at the four corners that served both decorative and functional purposes. Horns in ancient Near Eastern symbolism represented strength, power, and divine presence. The four-cornered design with horns at each corner created a sacred geometric form, likely representing completeness and cosmic order. The priest's precise application of blood to these horns—with his finger, marking all four points, then pouring the remainder at the base—created a complete sanctification of the altar. This procedure would have been visible and impressive to observing Israelites in the courtyard. The deliberateness and precision of the action communicated that atonement was not haphazard or magical but a carefully ordered covenant transaction governed by divine law.

word_study.meaning: blood; in Levitical theology, the life-force or vital essence of the flesh, which is the basis of atonement
word_study.significance: Dam is central to Levitical soteriology. Leviticus 17:11 explicitly states: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood...it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul.' Blood is not merely a physical substance but a covenant sign representing life itself. The priest's handling of blood—with reverent care and precise application—reflects the covenant's most sacred element. The term dam appears throughout Leviticus 4 with absolute consistency, emphasizing that regardless of which person brings the offering or which animal is sacrificed, the blood's atoning power is constant.

word_study.meaning: with his finger; the singular, intimate use of the priest's own digit rather than a vessel or instrument
word_study.significance: The use of the priest's finger creates personal agency and accountability. The priest is not merely pouring blood from a cup but applying it with bodily contact. This emphasizes the priest's role as mediator—his hands, his actions, his direct touch make the atonement effective. The finger is the instrument of precision, suggesting careful, intentional application. This detail appears in verses 6, 17, 25, 30, and 34—consistently in contexts requiring exactness in atonement.

word_study.meaning: the projecting corners of the altar, typically understood as four horn-like extensions at the cardinal points
word_study.significance: The horns were the altar's most sacred part—touching them was tantamount to touching God's dwelling place. In legal contexts, they provided refuge for the accused (1 Kings 1:50). By applying blood to the horns, the priest marks the altar as cleansed and fully operational. The four horns likely represent completeness and wholeness, covering all dimensions of the sanctified space. The outer altar (where v. 34 applies blood) had four horns; the inner altar (where vv. 7, 18 apply blood) also had four horns. The blood marking completes the altar's holiness.

word_study.meaning: to pour out, to shed, to spill; the pouring of remaining blood at the altar's base
word_study.significance: Shafakh is the verb for complete outpouring—nothing is withheld. The blood is poured 'at the bottom of the altar' (el yesod hamizbach), the foundation or base where it returns to the earth and God's domain. This action mirrors Deuteronomy 12:27, where the flesh is eaten but blood is 'poured out upon the altar of the LORD thy God.' The complete pouring ensures that the blood—the life-force—is fully surrendered to God.

word_study.meaning: the base or foundation of the altar, the ground-level where the blood ultimately reaches the earth
word_study.significance: The yesod (foundation) is where the altar connects to the earth and to God's realm. By pouring blood there, the priest ensures it reaches the deepest part of the sanctified space. The foundation receives the offering fully, making it inseparable from the altar's holiness. This is where the blood of all sin offerings goes—not into the air or the priests' hands, but into the earth beneath God's altar, acknowledged and received by God in his dwelling place.

commentary.application: Leviticus 4:34 teaches modern covenant members that atonement is not a distant, abstract transaction but a concrete reality that requires precise, mediated application. Just as the priest's finger—his personal agency and authorized role—applies the blood, modern Latter-day Saints access atonement through priesthood-administered covenants and ordinances. The specification that 'all the blood' be poured out—nothing withheld, nothing retained by the offerer—teaches the nature of genuine repentance: complete surrender, complete commitment, all offered to God. You cannot hold back part of your sin for yourself or hide some guilt while confessing other transgressions. Repentance is all or nothing. The horns of the altar being marked on all four sides teaches that atonement covers every aspect of your life—every thought, every action, every relationship. The pouring at the foundation—returning the blood to the earth—teaches that atonement is not a transaction that vanishes but one that reaches into the deepest levels of your soul and being, touching the very foundation of who you are. Through Christ's blood, that atonement reaches and cleanses you completely.
commentary.christological_typology: The priest's application of blood—marking the altar thoroughly and completely—prefigures Christ as both the eternal priest and the offering whose blood covers all sin. Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts the Levitical priest, who 'standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices,' with Christ, who 'offered one sacrifice for sins for ever.' The precision of blood application in verse 34, repeated thousands of times for each sin offering brought, points to the efficacy of Christ's single, perfect offering. The blood touching the altar's horns—its most sacred points—parallels how Christ's blood, applied once at Calvary, eternally sanctifies God's altar (the reconciliation between God and humanity). The completeness of the blood pouring ('all the blood thereof') suggests nothing is withheld; similarly, Christ withheld nothing from his sacrificial role, offering 'his whole soul as an offering for sin' (Isaiah 53:10).

text_kjv: And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat of the lamb is taken away from the sacrifice of the peace offerings; and the priest shall burn them upon the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the LORD: and the priest shall make an atonement for his sin that he hath committed, and it shall be forgiven him.

commentary.narrative: Verse 35 brings Leviticus 4 to its theological and structural conclusion. It is the fourth and final occurrence of the closing formula 'the priest shall make an atonement...and it shall be forgiven him' (kipper... veniselach lo)—a formula that appears identically in verses 20 (high priest), 26 (congregation), 31 (commoner with goat), and 35 (commoner with lamb). This repetition is not accidental or merely informative; it is the chapter's theological thesis. The translator notes are explicit: 'The chapter's final verse delivers the same verdict as v20, v26, and v31: kipper... veniselach lo—atonement and forgiveness. Four categories, four procedures, one outcome.' The graduated procedures for different offerers (bull for priest, bull for congregation, goat for leader, goat or lamb for commoner) do not produce graduated forgiveness. Every Israelite who brings the prescribed offering receives full, complete atonement and forgiveness. This is a revolutionary statement in the ancient religious world.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final verse parallels verse 31 almost exactly—both describe the commoner's sin offering, both involve fat removal compared to the peace offering, both conclude with identical forgiveness language. The reason for this repetition is pedagogical clarity: the Levitical system presents two economically accessible options for the commoner (goat in v. 28-31, lamb in v. 32-35), and by repeating the full procedure with identical results, the law affirms that the choice is purely economic, not theological. An Israelite of means can bring a goat; an Israelite of lesser means can bring a lamb. Either choice satisfies the covenant requirement completely. The instruction that the priest 'shall burn them upon the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the LORD' (vehiktir hakkohen otam hamizbacha al ishei YHWH) specifies that the fat portions burned are part of the fire offerings (ishim)—the offerings that are entirely consumed by fire on the altar.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The final phrase—'and the priest shall make an atonement for his sin that he hath committed, and it shall be forgiven him'—is the chapter's capstone. The addition of 'for his sin that he hath committed' (al-chattato asher chata) makes explicit what has been implicit throughout: the offering addresses a specific transgression, a particular sin that has defiled both the sinner and the sanctuary. The passive voice 'it shall be forgiven him' (veniselach lo) emphasizes God's action. The priest performs kipper (atonement), making the ritual action operative; God grants selach (forgiveness), removing the transgression. Together, they accomplish restoration: the sanctuary is cleansed (kipper), and the offerer is absolved (selach). Modern readers often miss the profound theological claim here: forgiveness is not earned by the offerer's effort, not determined by the quality of the offering, not contingent on the animal's size or cost. Forgiveness is granted when the prescribed covenant procedure is followed with sincerity. The system is structured to make atonement universally accessible and forgiveness divinely assured.

cross_references.connection: The high priest's sin offering conclusion uses identical kipper... veniselach lo formula, establishing that the priest and the commoner receive equivalent atonement despite their vastly different status and offering.
The congregation's sin offering conclusion uses the identical forgiveness formula, extending the principle of universal atonement beyond individual leaders to the entire covenant community.
The commoner's goat sin offering conclusion uses nearly identical language, confirming that the choice between goat and lamb does not alter the atonement's outcome.

The foundational principle that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood...it is the blood that makes an atonement for the soul'—the theological ground that makes the fat removal and blood application in verse 35 efficacious.

God 'hath not dealt with us after our sins...as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us'—the spiritual reality that the Levitical sin offering prefigures and enables.

Contrasts the Levitical priest's repetitive daily sacrifices with Christ's 'one sacrifice for sins for ever,' positioning the repeated sin offerings of Leviticus 4 as types of the ultimate, eternal offering.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:14-16 testifies that Christ 'shall be the source of our salvation, yea, even he in whom it is proper that man should put his trust...and this is according to the spirit of revelation which is in me.' The Book of Mormon explicitly identifies Christ as the sin offering's fulfillment. The Levitical system, repeated daily and yearly, is revealed in the Restoration to be preparatory—pointing toward 'that one offering for sins' (Hebrews 10:12) made once and for all in Christ. Verse 35's forgiveness formula finds its ultimate meaning in Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:42 states: 'Behold, I say unto you, that you must visit the poor and the needy and administer to their relief, that they may be kept until all things are made equal.' The Levitical system's graduated offerings, culminating in verse 35's universal forgiveness, anticipates the Doctrine and Covenants' principle that the covenant provides for all, especially the least advantaged.
